Part A · Foundations

How to Use This Handbook

This handbook is the single operating manual of the Web Development Engineering Department. It does two jobs: (1) it trains a beginner who knows basic computer operations into a professional who can join supervised client projects, and (2) it defines the mandatory 27-stage lifecycle every client project follows - with approval gates, deliverables and acceptance criteria - from the first enquiry to maintenance.

GOLDEN RULES

  1. Do not skip stages. Do not start a stage until the acceptance criteria of the previous stage are met and its gate is signed.
  2. "It runs on my laptop" is not "production-ready". Production-ready means secure, tested, monitored, backed up, restorable, documented, cost-controlled and handed over.
  3. Never commit credentials, private keys, production .env files or confidential customer data to Git, chat, e-mail or documents.
  4. Never run destructive commands (rm -rf, DROP DATABASE, git push --force) without understanding the effect and holding a verified backup.
  5. Every production change needs a second person's review.
  6. Never promise uptime, "unhackable" security, rankings or savings without evidence. We say what was tested - not that a system is "secure".
  7. Never invent prices. Quote only from official vendor pricing pages and calculators, with the date checked.

Part A · Foundations

1. Department and Service Portfolio

The Web Development Engineering Department builds, launches and maintains web products for business clients. Fourteen commercially deliverable services are offered. Each can be sold alone or combined, and each follows the same 27-stage lifecycle (Section 5) - the lifecycle is scaled to the project, never skipped.

SELECT TECHNOLOGY BY REQUIREMENT

We never force one stack on every client. A five-page brochure site does not need a Kubernetes cluster; a payment-processing SaaS does not belong on a 30-page WordPress theme. The Technical Lead records every stack decision in an Architecture Decision Record (Stage 09).

WHAT WE DO NOT DO

We do not copy a competitor's text, images or code. We do not build deceptive, illegal or privacy-violating systems. We do not store card numbers ourselves. We do not offer legal, tax or regulatory advice; we offer compliance-readiness support and say that certification and legal compliance are determined by qualified auditors and counsel. We never claim a system is "secure" or "guaranteed" - we state what was tested.

Part A · Foundations

2. Employee Onboarding Programme

The onboarding programme turns a new joiner into a safe, productive team member in the first 13 weeks. It combines access and policy setup (days 1-5), foundation learning (weeks 1-4) and supervised delivery (weeks 5-13). The detailed tick-list is Appendix A1; the week-by-week plan is Appendix A2.

Who you are on day one

You know basic computer operations - files, folders, browser, e-mail. You are not expected to know programming. The programme assumes zero professional web experience and builds from there. You will always work under a named mentor until you pass Gate 5 (week 13).

Study rhythm

Daily: 2 hours reading + 4 hours hands-on + 30 minutes writing notes in the training repository. Weekly: mentor review and one demonstration. Never copy-paste code you cannot explain line by line.

Level 1 - Web Fundamentals (about 2 weeks)

Goal: explain how the web works end to end and name the part where any given problem lives.

L1.1 · Internet and Web Architecture

EssentialFree3 h
1 · DefinitionThe internet is the global network of connected computers. The web is one service that runs on it - pages and apps delivered over HTTP. A web architecture is the set of parts (browser, DNS, CDN, server, application, database) that cooperate to answer one request.
2 · Business purposeEvery client problem ("the site is slow", "the form does not save") lives in one of these parts. An employee who can name the parts can find the fault in minutes instead of guessing for days.
3 · Real-world exampleA customer opens a bakery website. The browser asks DNS for the address, the CDN returns cached images, the web server passes the order form to the application, and the application saves the order in the database.
4 · PrerequisitesBasic computer use; ability to open a browser and a terminal.
5 · Tools & installationChrome or Firefox (free), a terminal (Windows Terminal/WSL, macOS Terminal, Linux shell), draw.io or Excalidraw (free) for diagrams.

6 · Step-by-step procedure

  1. Open any public website and open DevTools (F12), tab Network.
  2. Reload the page and list every request - note the first one (the HTML document) and the later ones (CSS, JS, images, API calls).
  3. Draw the path on paper - browser, DNS, CDN, server, app, database - and write one sentence per hop.
  4. Label where each request could fail (DNS error, TLS error, 404, 500, database timeout).

7 · Complete example

Browser --DNS lookup--> DNS resolver  (name -> IP)
Browser --HTTPS-------> CDN / WAF     (cache, DDoS filter)
CDN     --HTTP--------> Web server    (Nginx)
Web server ----------> Application    (Node.js / FastAPI)
Application ---SQL---> Database       (PostgreSQL)

8 · Expected output

A hand-drawn diagram with 6 boxes and arrows, plus a table:
Hop | What can fail | Symptom the client sees
DNS | wrong record | "Server not found"
TLS | expired certificate | browser security warning
App | unhandled exception | HTTP 500
9 · VerificationThe Technical Lead can pick any hop and the employee explains what it does and one way it fails.
10 · Common errorsTreating "the website" as one thing; confusing the web (HTTP) with the internet (all traffic); forgetting that a CDN may serve a stale copy.
11 · Security considerationsEvery hop is an attack surface. Only the web server/CDN should be public; the database must never be reachable from the internet.
12 · DocumentationSave the diagram as docs/architecture.md in the training repository.
13 · Practical assignmentChoose three real websites. For each, record in a table which hops you can identify from DevTools (CDN header, server header, API calls).
14 · Assessment10-question quiz (pass 80%) plus a 5-minute whiteboard of the request path.
15 · Approval gateTechnical Lead signs Level 1 checklist item 1.

Read: MDN - How the web works

L1.2 · Browser and Server

EssentialFree3 h
1 · DefinitionA browser is a client program that requests, downloads and renders web resources. A server is a computer or program that listens for requests and returns responses.
2 · Business purposeKnowing which side runs which code decides where bugs are fixed, where secrets may live and what the client can see.
3 · Real-world exampleHTML/CSS/JS download to every visitor and run in the browser (public). Python or Node code runs only on our server (private) and may use secret keys.
4 · PrerequisitesL1.1.
5 · Tools & installationBrowser DevTools; Node.js LTS (free) to run a tiny server; VS Code.

6 · Step-by-step procedure

  1. Install Node.js LTS and verify with node -v.
  2. Create server.js with the example below.
  3. Run node server.js and open http://localhost:3000.
  4. In DevTools > Network, click the request and read the request and response headers.

7 · Complete example

// server.js - a server is just a program that listens on a port
const http = require('node:http');
http.createServer((req, res) => {
  console.log(req.method, req.url);
  res.writeHead(200, { 'Content-Type': 'text/html; charset=utf-8' });
  res.end('<h1>Hello from the server</h1>');
}).listen(3000, () => console.log('Listening on http://localhost:3000'));

8 · Expected output

Terminal:  Listening on http://localhost:3000
Terminal:  GET /
Browser:   a page showing the heading "Hello from the server"
9 · VerificationChange the text, restart the server, reload the page; the new text appears. Stop the server and reload - the browser shows "connection refused".
10 · Common errorsPort already in use (EADDRINUSE); opening the file with file:// instead of http://; forgetting to restart after editing.
11 · Security considerationsNever put API keys in browser-delivered code - anyone can read it via View Source or DevTools.
12 · DocumentationREADME section "Run locally" with the exact commands.
13 · Practical assignmentExtend the server to return different text for /about and a 404 for unknown paths.
14 · AssessmentExplain in 3 sentences why a payment secret key cannot live in JavaScript sent to the browser.
15 · Approval gateDemo to a mentor; mentor signs the log.

L1.3 · HTTP and HTTPS

EssentialFree4 h
1 · DefinitionHTTP is the request/response protocol of the web: a method (GET, POST...), a path, headers and an optional body go out; a status code, headers and a body come back. HTTPS is HTTP inside a TLS-encrypted channel that also proves the server's identity with a certificate.
2 · Business purposeClients expect the padlock; search engines and browsers penalise plain HTTP; payment and login pages must be encrypted. Status codes are also the common language for debugging.
3 · Real-world exampleA login form sends POST /api/login. The server answers 200 with a cookie, or 401 if the password is wrong.
4 · PrerequisitesL1.2.
5 · Tools & installationcurl (preinstalled on most systems), browser DevTools, Postman (free tier).

6 · Step-by-step procedure

  1. Run curl -I https://example.com and read the status line and headers.
  2. Run curl -v https://example.com 2>&1 | head -30 and find the TLS handshake lines.
  3. Request a path that does not exist and record the status code.
  4. Memorise the status families - 2xx success, 3xx redirect, 4xx client error, 5xx server error.

7 · Complete example

curl -I https://example.com               # headers only
curl -i https://example.com/missing-page   # headers + body of a 404
curl -X POST https://httpbin.org/post -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"name":"Asha"}'

8 · Expected output

HTTP/2 200
content-type: text/html
cache-control: max-age=...
(exact headers vary by site and date)
9 · VerificationFor five different URLs, state the status code before you run curl, then confirm.
10 · Common errorsConfusing 401 (not logged in) with 403 (logged in but not allowed); using GET to change data; ignoring redirect chains (301 > 302 > 200).
11 · Security considerationsRedirect all HTTP to HTTPS; enable HSTS only after HTTPS works everywhere; never send passwords in a URL query string.
12 · DocumentationTable of the status codes our APIs return, kept in docs/api-specification.md.
13 · Practical assignmentMake a one-page cheat sheet - 10 status codes, when we use each, example response body.
14 · AssessmentQuiz - choose the correct status for 12 scenarios (e.g. validation failed = 422/400, duplicate email = 409).
15 · Approval gateQuiz pass (80%) recorded by the Technical Lead.

Read: MDN - HTTP

L1.4 · DNS and Domains

EssentialPaid3 h
1 · DefinitionDNS (Domain Name System) translates names such as example.com into IP addresses. A domain is a name registered through a registrar. Common records: A (IPv4), AAAA (IPv6), CNAME (alias), MX (mail), TXT (verification, SPF/DKIM).
2 · Business purposeWrong DNS is the most common cause of "the new site is not showing" and "emails go to spam". Domain ownership must also be in the client's name.
3 · Real-world exampleWe deploy the client site to 203.0.113.10. We add an A record www -> 203.0.113.10 at the registrar; within the TTL, visitors reach the site.
4 · PrerequisitesL1.3.
5 · Tools & installationdig or nslookup; a registrar account (paid, usually yearly); Cloudflare DNS (free plan available - verify current plan terms).

6 · Step-by-step procedure

  1. Run dig example.com A +short and dig example.com MX +short.
  2. Find the nameservers with dig example.com NS +short.
  3. In a sandbox domain (or Cloudflare test zone), add an A record and a CNAME and watch propagation with dig.
  4. Lower the TTL to 300 seconds 24 hours before any planned cut-over.

7 · Complete example

dig yourdomain.com A +short
dig www.yourdomain.com CNAME +short
dig yourdomain.com MX +short
nslookup yourdomain.com 1.1.1.1

8 · Expected output

203.0.113.10            <- A record (documentation IP - yours will differ)
yourdomain.com.         <- CNAME target
10 mail.provider.net.   <- MX priority + host
9 · VerificationThe record returned by two different public resolvers (1.1.1.1 and 8.8.8.8) matches what you configured.
10 · Common errorsEditing records at the wrong place (registrar vs. DNS host); CNAME on the root domain; forgetting www; expecting instant propagation.
11 · Security considerationsEnable registrar lock and 2FA; domain registered to the client, never an employee's personal account; keep a record of renewal dates.
12 · DocumentationDNS record table in docs/deployment.md - type, name, value, TTL, owner, date.
13 · Practical assignmentWrite the DNS plan for a client migrating from shared hosting to a new server with zero email downtime.
14 · AssessmentGiven five broken-symptom scenarios, name the record type to inspect.
15 · Approval gateMentor review of the DNS plan.

Read: MDN - What is a domain name

L1.5 · Hosting

EssentialPaid4 h
1 · DefinitionHosting is the computer and network capacity that runs a website. Models: static/CDN hosting, shared hosting, VPS, managed platform (PaaS), containers, serverless, and dedicated cloud.
2 · Business purposeThe hosting choice sets cost, speed, security and maintenance effort for years. It must match the project, not the developer's habit.
3 · Real-world exampleA 5-page brochure site goes on static hosting + CDN. A booking system with a database goes on a managed platform or a small cloud VM with automated backups.
4 · PrerequisitesL1.4.
5 · Tools & installationCloudflare Pages, Vercel, Netlify, AWS, Azure, GCP, DigitalOcean, a cPanel host. Free tiers exist but limits and prices change - check the vendor's current pricing page.

6 · Step-by-step procedure

  1. Classify the project - static, dynamic, or stateful with a database.
  2. List non-functional needs - traffic, uptime target, data location, budget, who maintains it.
  3. Compare three hosts in a table (cost, backup, scaling, region, support) using each vendor's official pricing page and record the date.
  4. Pick one and write the reason in an Architecture Decision Record.

7 · Complete example

ADR-001: Hosting choice
Context : 8-page site + contact form, ~2,000 visits/month, owner non-technical
Options : A static host + serverless form   B shared hosting   C VPS
Decision: A - lowest maintenance, automatic TLS, global CDN
Consequences: form handled by serverless function; no server patching by us
Verified pricing on: <date> from <vendor pricing URL>

8 · Expected output

A one-page comparison table and a signed ADR stored in `docs/adr/`.
9 · VerificationAnother employee can re-derive the same cost figure from the linked vendor page.
10 · Common errorsChoosing by price alone; ignoring bandwidth/egress charges; no backup on a VPS; quoting prices from memory.
11 · Security considerationsLeast-privilege access; separate accounts per environment; automatic OS and runtime patching decided before go-live.
12 · DocumentationADR + cost table in docs/architecture.md.
13 · Practical assignmentProduce hosting recommendations for three client types - dentist brochure site, online shop, SaaS dashboard.
14 · AssessmentTech Lead questions the ADR for 10 minutes; employee defends the decision.
15 · Approval gateADR approved by Technical Lead.

L1.6 · Frontend and Backend

EssentialFree3 h
1 · DefinitionThe frontend is everything the user sees and interacts with in the browser (HTML, CSS, JavaScript/TypeScript, React). The backend is the server-side code and services that apply business rules, talk to the database and protect secrets.
2 · Business purposeClear separation lets frontend and backend developers work in parallel, lets us change one without breaking the other, and keeps secrets safe.
3 · Real-world exampleFrontend: a booking form validates the date for convenience. Backend: re-validates the date, checks the slot is free, charges the card, saves the booking.
4 · PrerequisitesL1.2, L1.3.
5 · Tools & installationVS Code, Node.js LTS, a browser.

6 · Step-by-step procedure

  1. Take a feature such as "add to cart".
  2. List what the frontend does (button, UI state, call API).
  3. List what the backend does (check stock, price, save, respond).
  4. Mark every rule that must be enforced on the server even if the browser also checks it.

7 · Complete example

FEATURE: Apply discount code
Frontend : input box, "Apply" button, show new total, show error text
Backend  : find code, check expiry + usage limit + minimum order,
           recalculate total from DB prices (never trust browser total),
           store discount on the order, return updated total
Rule     : price and discount are ALWAYS computed on the server

8 · Expected output

A two-column responsibility table for three features of your choice.
9 · VerificationMentor picks one rule; employee shows where it is enforced on the server.
10 · Common errorsTrusting browser-supplied prices or roles; duplicating business rules in both places and letting them drift.
11 · Security considerationsAll validation is repeated on the server; frontend validation is only for user comfort.
12 · DocumentationResponsibility table in the feature's section of docs/requirements.md.
13 · Practical assignmentSplit "user registration with email verification" into frontend/backend tasks with estimates.
14 · AssessmentThree scenario questions - where does this logic belong and why.
15 · Approval gateMentor sign-off.

L1.7 · Databases (concepts)

EssentialFree3 h
1 · DefinitionA database is organised, durable storage for application data. A relational database (PostgreSQL, MySQL) stores rows in tables linked by keys and is queried with SQL. Other types (document, key-value, search) exist for specific needs.
2 · Business purposeBusiness data - customers, orders, bookings - is the client's most valuable asset. Wrong design is expensive to fix later; lost data is a business-ending event.
3 · Real-world exampleA shop has customers, orders and order_items tables. One customer can have many orders; each order has many items.
4 · PrerequisitesL1.6.
5 · Tools & installationSQLite (built in to Python, free) for first exercises; later PostgreSQL.

6 · Step-by-step procedure

  1. Choose a business (clinic, school, shop) and list the "things" it tracks (entities).
  2. For each entity list its attributes and a unique identifier.
  3. Draw relationships (one-to-many, many-to-many).
  4. Create the tables in SQLite and insert 5 sample rows each.

7 · Complete example

import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE customers(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, email TEXT UNIQUE NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE orders(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id), total_minor INTEGER NOT NULL);
INSERT INTO customers(name,email) VALUES ('Asha','asha@example.com');
INSERT INTO orders(customer_id,total_minor) VALUES (1, 129900);
""")
print(db.execute("SELECT c.name, o.total_minor FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id=o.customer_id").fetchall())

8 · Expected output

[('Asha', 129900)]
9 · VerificationTry inserting an order with customer_id = 99 - the database rejects it (foreign key). Insert a duplicate email - rejected (UNIQUE).
10 · Common errorsStoring money as floating point (use integer minor units or DECIMAL); storing comma-separated lists in one column; no primary key.
11 · Security considerationsNever expose a database port to the internet; use a dedicated low-privilege application user; never string-concatenate SQL.
12 · DocumentationER diagram in docs/database-design.md.
13 · Practical assignmentModel a clinic appointment system with at least five tables.
14 · AssessmentWhiteboard review - find three weaknesses in a deliberately flawed schema.
15 · Approval gateMentor approves the ER diagram.

L1.8 · APIs

EssentialFree3 h
1 · DefinitionAn API (Application Programming Interface) is a defined way for one program to talk to another. A REST API exposes resources at URLs (/api/products/12) and uses HTTP methods - GET (read), POST (create), PUT/PATCH (update), DELETE (remove) - usually exchanging JSON.
2 · Business purposeThe frontend, mobile apps, payment providers and the client's other systems all connect through APIs. A clear contract lets teams build in parallel.
3 · Real-world exampleThe shop frontend calls GET /api/products?category=shoes and receives a JSON list it renders as cards.
4 · PrerequisitesL1.3, L1.6.
5 · Tools & installationPostman (free tier) or curl; the public JSONPlaceholder test API; browser DevTools.

6 · Step-by-step procedure

  1. Call a public API with GET and read the JSON.
  2. Call it with POST and a JSON body.
  3. Record method, URL, headers, body, status and response in a Postman collection.
  4. Write the contract for one new endpoint before any code exists.

7 · Complete example

curl -s https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts/1
curl -s -X POST https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"title":"Hello","body":"First post","userId":1}'

8 · Expected output

{
  "userId": 1,
  "id": 1,
  "title": "sunt aut facere ...",
  "body": "quia et suscipit ..."
}
(second call returns the created object with "id": 101)
9 · VerificationYour Postman collection runs end to end with no manual edits.
10 · Common errorsMissing Content-Type header; sending invalid JSON (trailing comma); treating a 200 with an error message as success.
11 · Security considerationsAPIs need authentication, authorisation, rate limits and validation (OWASP API Security Top 10).
12 · DocumentationEndpoint table - method, path, auth, request, response, errors - in docs/api-specification.md.
13 · Practical assignmentDesign (on paper) a REST API for a library - books, members, loans - with request/response examples.
14 · AssessmentReview a flawed API (verbs in URLs, wrong status codes) and list corrections.
15 · Approval gateTech Lead reviews API design.

Read: OWASP API Security Top 10

L1.9 · Responsive Design (concepts)

EssentialFree3 h
1 · DefinitionResponsive design makes one site work well on every screen size - phone, tablet, laptop, large monitor - using flexible layouts, flexible media and CSS media queries. The strategy is mobile-first: design for the smallest screen, then enhance.
2 · Business purposeMost client traffic is on phones. A site that needs pinch-zoom loses customers and search ranking.
3 · Real-world exampleA three-column feature grid collapses to one column on a 360 px phone, two on a tablet and three on a desktop.
4 · PrerequisitesL1.6.
5 · Tools & installationBrowser DevTools device toolbar, a real phone, Lighthouse (built into Chrome DevTools).

6 · Step-by-step procedure

  1. Add <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1"> to every page.
  2. Use relative units (rem, %, fr) and max-width, not fixed pixel widths.
  3. Write base CSS for 360 px, then add @media (min-width: 768px) and (min-width: 1024px) enhancements.
  4. Test at 360, 768, 1024 and 1440 px, then on a real phone.

7 · Complete example

.grid { display: grid; gap: 1rem; grid-template-columns: 1fr; }
@media (min-width: 768px)  { .grid { grid-template-columns: repeat(2, 1fr); } }
@media (min-width: 1024px) { .grid { grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr); } }
img { max-width: 100%; height: auto; }

8 · Expected output

1 column at 360 px, 2 columns at 800 px, 3 columns at 1200 px; no horizontal scrollbar at any width.
9 · VerificationDevTools responsive mode at the four widths plus Lighthouse "Best practices/Accessibility" with no layout errors.
10 · Common errorsMissing viewport meta tag; fixed-width elements causing horizontal scroll; tap targets smaller than about 44 px; text under 16 px on phones.
11 · Security considerationsNot directly security-related - but hidden mobile menus must remain keyboard accessible.
12 · DocumentationList the breakpoints chosen in docs/architecture.md (frontend section).
13 · Practical assignmentConvert a fixed 960 px desktop layout to responsive using only CSS.
14 · AssessmentPractical test - given a broken page, fix it at all four widths in 30 minutes.
15 · Approval gateLevel 1 completion review - all nine modules signed, quiz average at least 80%.

Read: web.dev - Learn Responsive Design

Level 2 - Frontend Development (about 5 weeks)

Goal: build responsive, accessible, fast user interfaces with HTML, CSS, JavaScript, TypeScript, React and Next.js.

L2.1 · HTML5

EssentialFree6 h
1 · DefinitionHTML (HyperText Markup Language) describes the structure and meaning of a page using elements such as <header>, <nav>, <main>, <h1>, <p>, <img>, <a> and <form>. HTML5 added semantic elements, native media and form controls.
2 · Business purposeCorrect semantic HTML gives accessibility, SEO and maintainability for free. Clients lose search traffic when pages are built from anonymous <div> soup.
3 · Real-world exampleA clinic homepage uses one <h1>, a <nav> with a list of links, <main> with sections, and a <footer> with address markup - screen readers and Google both understand it.
4 · PrerequisitesLevel 1 complete.
5 · Tools & installationVS Code with Live Server and Prettier extensions; Chrome; the W3C Nu HTML Checker (free, online).

6 · Step-by-step procedure

  1. Create index.html with <!doctype html>, lang, charset and viewport meta tags.
  2. Build the layout with <header>, <nav>, <main>, <section>, <article>, <footer>.
  3. Add one <h1> and a logical heading order (h2 under h1, h3 under h2).
  4. Add images with meaningful alt, a contact form with <label for> on every input.
  5. Validate with the W3C checker and fix every error.

7 · Complete example

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>Sunrise Dental Clinic - Chennai</title>
  <meta name="description" content="Family dentistry with online booking.">
</head>
<body>
  <header><nav aria-label="Main"><a href="/">Home</a> <a href="/services">Services</a></nav></header>
  <main>
    <h1>Gentle dentistry for the whole family</h1>
    <form action="/api/contact" method="post">
      <label for="email">Email</label>
      <input id="email" name="email" type="email" required autocomplete="email">
      <button type="submit">Request a call</button>
    </form>
  </main>
  <footer><p>&copy; 2026 Sunrise Dental</p></footer>
</body>
</html>

8 · Expected output

A page with a heading, a labelled email field and a button; zero errors in the W3C validator.
9 · VerificationTab through the page with the keyboard - every link and control gets a visible focus; Lighthouse accessibility score at least 90.
10 · Common errorsSkipping heading levels for styling; <div> instead of <button>; missing alt; placeholder used instead of label; duplicate ids.
11 · Security considerationsNever build HTML by concatenating untrusted text (XSS). Add rel="noopener noreferrer" on target="_blank" links.
12 · DocumentationPage templates and component notes in frontend/README.md.
13 · Practical assignmentBuild a one-page business site (header, hero, services list, contact form, footer) using only semantic HTML.
14 · AssessmentMentor opens the page with CSS disabled - the content must still read in a sensible order.
15 · Approval gateZero validator errors; mentor sign-off.

Read: MDN - HTML · HTML Living Standard

L2.2 · CSS3

EssentialFree8 h
1 · DefinitionCSS (Cascading Style Sheets) controls presentation - colour, type, spacing, layout, animation. Key ideas are the cascade and specificity, the box model (content, padding, border, margin), custom properties (--brand) and units (rem, %, vw).
2 · Business purposeConsistent, maintainable CSS makes a client's brand look right on every page and keeps later redesigns cheap.
3 · Real-world exampleOne --brand colour variable changes the whole site's buttons, links and focus rings in a single edit.
4 · PrerequisitesL2.1.
5 · Tools & installationVS Code, DevTools Elements/Styles panel, Stylelint (optional).

6 · Step-by-step procedure

  1. Add a reset (box-sizing:border-box) and define design tokens as CSS variables.
  2. Style type scale and spacing with rem units.
  3. Style components with simple class selectors (avoid deep nesting and !important).
  4. Add states - :hover, :focus-visible, :disabled.
  5. Inspect an element and read which rule wins and why.

7 · Complete example

:root { --brand:#14306b; --accent:#c2185b; --space:1rem; --radius:.5rem; }
*,*::before,*::after { box-sizing: border-box; }
body { margin:0; font:1rem/1.5 system-ui, sans-serif; color:#171c28; }
.btn { background:var(--brand); color:#fff; padding:.6rem 1.1rem; border:0; border-radius:var(--radius); }
.btn:hover { background:var(--accent); }
.btn:focus-visible { outline:3px solid var(--accent); outline-offset:2px; }

8 · Expected output

A navy button that turns magenta on hover and shows a visible outline on keyboard focus.
9 · VerificationChange --brand once and confirm every component updates; contrast checker shows at least 4.5:1 for body text.
10 · Common errorsOver-specific selectors; magic pixel numbers; removing the focus outline; relying on !important.
11 · Security considerationsAvoid loading CSS from untrusted origins; do not inline user-supplied styles.
12 · DocumentationList the design tokens (colours, spacing, type) in frontend/README.md.
13 · Practical assignmentStyle the L2.1 page to match a provided mock-up within a 2 px tolerance.
14 · AssessmentTimed task - make a given unstyled form look like a design and fix three CSS bugs.
15 · Approval gateMentor sign-off against the mock-up.

Read: MDN - CSS

L2.3 · JavaScript

EssentialFree14 h
1 · DefinitionJavaScript is the programming language of the browser (and, with Node.js, of servers). Core ideas are variables (const, let), functions, arrays and objects, the DOM, events, fetch and asynchronous code (Promise, async/await).
2 · Business purposeJavaScript makes pages interactive - menus, forms, filters, carts - and is the foundation of React, Next.js and Node.
3 · Real-world exampleA booking form fetches free slots from the API when the date changes and shows them without reloading the page.
4 · PrerequisitesL2.1, L2.2.
5 · Tools & installationVS Code, Node.js LTS, browser console, ESLint + Prettier.

6 · Step-by-step procedure

  1. Learn values, functions, arrays (map, filter, reduce) and objects.
  2. Select elements and respond to events.
  3. Fetch JSON from an API with async/await and handle errors.
  4. Update the page safely using textContent (not innerHTML with user data).

7 · Complete example

const list = document.querySelector('#posts');
async function load() {
  try {
    const res = await fetch('https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts?_limit=3');
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
    const posts = await res.json();
    list.replaceChildren(...posts.map(p => {
      const li = document.createElement('li');
      li.textContent = p.title;           // textContent = safe against XSS
      return li;
    }));
  } catch (err) {
    list.textContent = 'Could not load posts. Please retry.';
    console.error(err);
  }
}
document.querySelector('#reload').addEventListener('click', load);
load();

8 · Expected output

Three post titles appear as list items; with the network disabled the friendly error message appears instead.
9 · VerificationRun ESLint with no errors; test the success and failure paths in DevTools (offline mode).
10 · Common errorsForgetting await; mutating shared state; using == instead of ===; not handling a failed fetch; blocking the page with a long loop.
11 · Security considerationsXSS - never insert untrusted data with innerHTML; never store tokens in localStorage for sensitive apps if httpOnly cookies are possible.
12 · DocumentationJSDoc comments on shared helpers; a short "how it works" note per feature.
13 · Practical assignmentBuild a task list - add, complete, delete, filter, persist to localStorage.
14 · AssessmentCode review of a 60-line script with seeded bugs; find at least 5.
15 · Approval gateMentor code review passed; 20-question quiz at least 80%.

Read: MDN - JavaScript

L2.4 · TypeScript

EssentialFree8 h
1 · DefinitionTypeScript is JavaScript plus a static type system. Types are checked at build time and erased before the code runs, so the browser still executes plain JavaScript.
2 · Business purposeTypes catch whole classes of bugs before the client sees them, make refactoring safe and document the shape of API data. Our standard for all new projects.
3 · Real-world exampleA function price(order: Order) refuses to compile if someone passes { total: '12' } where a number is required.
4 · PrerequisitesL2.3.
5 · Tools & installationNode.js LTS, npm i -D typescript, VS Code (built-in TS support), tsc --noEmit.

6 · Step-by-step procedure

  1. Run npx tsc --init, then enable "strict": true.
  2. Model API data with interface/type, unions and optional properties.
  3. Avoid any; use unknown and narrow with checks.
  4. Share types between frontend and backend or generate them from the API schema.

7 · Complete example

type Role = 'admin' | 'staff' | 'customer';
interface User { id: number; email: string; role: Role; phone?: string }

function canRefund(user: User): boolean {
  return user.role === 'admin' || user.role === 'staff';
}

const u: User = { id: 1, email: 'asha@example.com', role: 'customer' };
console.log(canRefund(u));          // false
// canRefund({ id: 2, email: 'x', role: 'owner' })  -> compile error: 'owner' is not a Role

8 · Expected output

`false` at runtime; the commented line fails with TS2322 when uncommented.
9 · Verificationnpx tsc --noEmit reports zero errors in CI.
10 · Common errorsSilencing errors with any or as; disabling strict mode; types that do not match the real API response.
11 · Security considerationsTypes do not validate runtime data - validate untrusted input at the boundary (e.g. with Zod/Pydantic) before trusting the types.
12 · DocumentationDocument shared types in docs/api-specification.md.
13 · Practical assignmentConvert the L2.3 task list to TypeScript with strict mode and zero any.
14 · AssessmentFix 10 compiler errors in a supplied project without using any.
15 · Approval gateCI type-check passes; mentor review.

Read: TypeScript Handbook

L2.5 · Responsive Layouts - Flexbox and Grid

EssentialFree8 h
1 · DefinitionFlexbox lays items out along one axis (a row or a column) and distributes spare space. CSS Grid lays out in two dimensions - rows and columns - and is ideal for page and card layouts.
2 · Business purposeThese two systems replace floats and tables, and produce layouts that adapt to every screen with very little CSS.
3 · Real-world exampleA header uses Flexbox (logo left, menu right). A product catalogue uses Grid with auto-fit so the number of columns adapts to screen width automatically.
4 · PrerequisitesL2.2, L1.9.
5 · Tools & installationDevTools Flexbox/Grid overlays; Flexbox Froggy and Grid Garden (free games).

6 · Step-by-step procedure

  1. Build a header with display:flex; justify-content:space-between; align-items:center.
  2. Build a card grid with repeat(auto-fit, minmax(240px, 1fr)).
  3. Add gap instead of margins between items.
  4. Test at 360, 768, 1024 and 1440 px.

7 · Complete example

.site-header { display:flex; justify-content:space-between; align-items:center; gap:1rem; flex-wrap:wrap; }
.cards { display:grid; gap:1rem; grid-template-columns:repeat(auto-fit, minmax(240px, 1fr)); }
.card { padding:1rem; border:1px solid #d5dcea; border-radius:.75rem; }

8 · Expected output

1 card per row at 360 px, 2-3 at tablet widths, 4 on wide screens, with no media query.
9 · VerificationNo horizontal scroll at any width from 320 px to 1600 px.
10 · Common errorsFixed heights that clip text; forgetting flex-wrap; nested grids too deep; using Grid for everything or Flexbox for everything.
11 · Security considerationsNone specific.
12 · DocumentationLayout rules recorded in the frontend README (which pattern for which component).
13 · Practical assignmentRebuild a 3-section landing page (hero, features, pricing, footer) that is fully responsive.
14 · AssessmentReproduce a given responsive mock-up in 45 minutes.
15 · Approval gateMentor sign-off at four widths.

Read: MDN - CSS layout

L2.6 · Accessibility

EssentialFree6 h
1 · DefinitionAccessibility (a11y) means people with disabilities can perceive, operate and understand the site - keyboard-only users, screen-reader users, low-vision and colour-blind users. The standard is WCAG 2.2 (target level AA).
2 · Business purposeAccessibility is a quality requirement, widens the client's audience and, in many markets, a legal expectation. Fixing it late costs far more than building it in.
3 · Real-world exampleA customer who cannot use a mouse can still open the menu, fill the booking form and pay, using only Tab, Enter and Space.
4 · PrerequisitesL2.1, L2.2.
5 · Tools & installationLighthouse, axe DevTools extension (free), NVDA (Windows, free) or VoiceOver (macOS), WebAIM contrast checker.

6 · Step-by-step procedure

  1. Use semantic elements first; add ARIA only when HTML cannot express the meaning.
  2. Make every control keyboard reachable with a visible :focus-visible style.
  3. Give each image a text alternative (empty alt="" for decorative images).
  4. Ensure text contrast of at least 4.5:1 and never use colour alone to convey meaning.
  5. Associate error messages with inputs using aria-describedby.

7 · Complete example

<label for="phone">Phone</label>
<input id="phone" name="phone" inputmode="tel" aria-describedby="phone-err" aria-invalid="true">
<p id="phone-err" role="alert">Enter a 10-digit mobile number.</p>
<button type="button" aria-expanded="false" aria-controls="menu">Menu</button>

8 · Expected output

A screen reader announces "Phone, edit text, invalid entry, Enter a 10-digit mobile number."
9 · Verificationaxe reports zero critical/serious issues; the whole flow works with the keyboard only; NVDA/VoiceOver read the form logically.
10 · Common errorsClick handlers on <div>; removing outlines; vague link text such as "click here"; images of text; autoplaying media.
11 · Security considerationsCAPTCHAs must have accessible alternatives; do not rely on hover for critical actions.
12 · DocumentationAccessibility statement and known issues in docs/user-guide.md.
13 · Practical assignmentAudit a sample site with axe and manual keyboard test; write a prioritised fix list.
14 · AssessmentFix the audit's top 10 issues in a given codebase.
15 · Approval gateAccessibility checklist in QA (Appendix A6) fully passed on your Level 2 project.

Read: web.dev - Learn Accessibility · MDN - Accessibility

L2.7 · Browser Developer Tools

EssentialFree4 h
1 · DefinitionDevTools are the debugging suite built into the browser - Elements (DOM/CSS), Console, Network, Sources (breakpoints), Application (storage, cookies), Performance and Lighthouse.
2 · Business purposeDevTools is the fastest way to reproduce and explain a bug to a client or colleague, and the main instrument for performance and accessibility checks.
3 · Real-world exampleA client says "the page is slow". The Network tab shows a 4 MB uncompressed hero image; compressing it to WebP cuts load time by seconds.
4 · PrerequisitesL2.1 to L2.3.
5 · Tools & installationChrome or Edge DevTools (F12), Firefox DevTools.

6 · Step-by-step procedure

  1. Elements - change CSS live and copy the working rule back to your code.
  2. Console - read errors; run small experiments.
  3. Network - throttle to "Fast 4G", disable cache, sort by size and time.
  4. Sources - set a breakpoint, step through a function.
  5. Application - inspect cookies and localStorage.
  6. Lighthouse - run a mobile audit and read the opportunities.

7 · Complete example

// Paste into the Console to find images that are too large for their display size
[...document.images]
  .filter(i => i.naturalWidth > i.clientWidth * 2)
  .map(i => ({ src: i.currentSrc, natural: i.naturalWidth, shown: i.clientWidth }));

8 · Expected output

An array of image objects (empty if all images are sized well).
9 · VerificationYou can reproduce one bug using only DevTools and record a screenshot of the failing request or console error.
10 · Common errorsTesting with cache enabled; testing only on a fast desktop connection; editing in DevTools and forgetting to copy the change back.
11 · Security considerationsDo not paste unknown scripts into the console (self-XSS). Never share screenshots or HAR files that contain tokens or cookies.
12 · DocumentationA "debugging notes" file in the training repo showing three bugs and how DevTools found them.
13 · Practical assignmentTake a slow public page you do not own (read-only analysis) and write a 1-page performance finding with screenshots.
14 · AssessmentMentor plants three bugs - find them using only DevTools in 20 minutes.
15 · Approval gateMentor sign-off.

Read: Chrome DevTools docs · web.dev - Performance

L2.8 · React

EssentialFree24 h
1 · DefinitionReact is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces from reusable components. A component is a function that takes props and returns UI; state (useState) holds data that changes; hooks (useEffect, custom hooks) share behaviour.
2 · Business purposeReact lets a team build large interactive applications - dashboards, portals, shops - from small, tested, reusable parts, and has the largest ecosystem and hiring pool.
3 · Real-world exampleA <ProductCard> component is reused in the catalogue, search results and the "recently viewed" strip; fix its layout once and every place updates.
4 · PrerequisitesL2.3, L2.4.
5 · Tools & installationNode.js LTS, Vite (npm create vite@latest), React DevTools extension, Vitest or Jest, React Testing Library.

6 · Step-by-step procedure

  1. Scaffold with Vite using the React + TypeScript template.
  2. Create a typed component with props and local state.
  3. Fetch data in an effect or a data library and render loading, error and empty states.
  4. Lift state up instead of duplicating it; keep components small.
  5. Write a test with React Testing Library.

7 · Complete example

import { useState } from 'react';

type Props = { name: string; price: number };

export function ProductCard({ name, price }: Props) {
  const [qty, setQty] = useState(1);
  return (
    <article className="card">
      <h2>{name}</h2>
      <p>Rs {(price * qty).toLocaleString('en-IN')}</p>
      <button onClick={() => setQty(q => q + 1)} aria-label={`Add one more ${name}`}>+</button>
      <span aria-live="polite">Qty {qty}</span>
    </article>
  );
}

8 · Expected output

A card showing the product name and a total that updates when "+" is pressed; the quantity change is announced to screen readers.
9 · Verificationnpm run build succeeds; component test passes; React DevTools shows the expected props and state.
10 · Common errorsMutating state directly; missing key in lists; effects with missing dependencies; fetching in a loop; giant components.
11 · Security considerationsReact escapes text by default; never use dangerouslySetInnerHTML with untrusted content; keep secrets out of the client bundle (only VITE_/NEXT_PUBLIC_ variables are public).
12 · DocumentationComponent catalogue (name, props, usage) in frontend/README.md; use Storybook where the project justifies it.
13 · Practical assignmentBuild a product catalogue with search, filter, cart state and a responsive layout.
14 · AssessmentCode review against the delivery standard (Section 7); mentor adds three change requests to implement in 2 hours.
15 · Approval gatePassed review; tests green; Lighthouse accessibility at least 90.

Read: React - Learn

L2.9 · Next.js (and when to choose alternatives)

EssentialFree16 h
1 · DefinitionNext.js is a React framework that adds file-based routing, server rendering (SSR), static generation (SSG), API/route handlers, image optimisation and deployment tooling. Alternatives - Astro (content sites), Remix/React Router, Vite + React SPA, Nuxt/SvelteKit (other ecosystems), WordPress (CMS-led sites).
2 · Business purposeSEO-critical, fast, full-stack React apps need server rendering and good defaults. Choosing the framework per project (not by habit) saves cost and avoids over-engineering.
3 · Real-world exampleA marketing site with a blog uses Astro or Next.js static export on a CDN. A logged-in customer portal uses Next.js with server components and an API.
4 · PrerequisitesL2.8.
5 · Tools & installationNode.js LTS, npx create-next-app@latest, Vercel / Cloudflare / Docker for deployment.

6 · Step-by-step procedure

  1. Create a project and read the generated folder structure (app/, public/).
  2. Add a route (app/services/page.tsx) and a shared layout.
  3. Fetch data on the server and render it; add metadata for SEO.
  4. Add a route handler for a form endpoint and validate input.
  5. Run npm run build and npm start to test the production build.

7 · Complete example

// app/services/page.tsx  (server component by default)
export const metadata = { title: 'Services - Sunrise Dental', description: 'Check-ups, whitening, implants.' };

async function getServices() {
  const res = await fetch(`${process.env.API_URL}/services`, { next: { revalidate: 300 } });
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error('Failed to load services');
  return res.json() as Promise<{ id: number; name: string }[]>;
}

export default async function ServicesPage() {
  const services = await getServices();
  return <ul>{services.map(s => <li key={s.id}>{s.name}</li>)}</ul>;
}

8 · Expected output

`/services` returns fully rendered HTML (View Source shows the list) and refreshes its cache every 5 minutes.
9 · VerificationLighthouse SEO at least 90; View Source contains the content; npm run build has no errors.
10 · Common errorsPutting secrets in NEXT_PUBLIC_ variables; mixing server and client code; fetching the same data repeatedly; skipping loading/error states.
11 · Security considerationsValidate every route handler input; add security headers; keep server-only code out of client components; protect authenticated routes on the server.
12 · DocumentationRendering strategy per page (static, server, client) in docs/architecture.md.
13 · Practical assignmentBuild the multi-page corporate website (Project 2) with SEO metadata, sitemap and optimised images.
14 · AssessmentExplain, for five pages, which rendering mode you chose and why.
15 · Approval gateLevel 2 completion review - modules signed, Project 1 and 2 accepted.

Read: Next.js docs · Astro docs

Level 3 - Backend Development (about 4 weeks)

Goal: build secure, tested, documented APIs with authentication, authorisation, validation and business logic.

L3.1 · Backend Framework and Your First API

EssentialFree12 h
1 · DefinitionA backend framework gives routing, request parsing, validation, dependency handling and error responses so we do not rebuild them. Our primary options are FastAPI (Python, typed, auto-documented), Django (Python, batteries-included with ORM and admin), and Node.js with Express/Fastify/NestJS.
2 · Business purposeThe framework sets how fast the team builds, how easy the code is to test and how well the API is documented. We pick per project - FastAPI for API-first products, Django when an admin panel and ORM save time, Node when the team is TypeScript end-to-end.
3 · Real-world exampleA booking platform uses FastAPI for the API (automatic OpenAPI docs the frontend team reads) and Next.js for the UI.
4 · PrerequisitesLevel 2 modules L2.3 and L2.4; Python 3.11+ or Node LTS installed.
5 · Tools & installationPython 3.11+, pip/venv (or uv), fastapi, uvicorn, pytest, httpx; Postman. Django alternative - django, djangorestframework. Node alternative - Fastify or NestJS.

6 · Step-by-step procedure

  1. Create a virtual environment and install fastapi and uvicorn[standard].
  2. Write main.py with a health endpoint and a create/read endpoint.
  3. Run uvicorn main:app --reload and open /docs (Swagger UI).
  4. Write a pytest using TestClient.

7 · Complete example

# main.py - run with: uvicorn main:app --reload
from fastapi import FastAPI, HTTPException
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

app = FastAPI(title="Clinic API", version="0.1.0")

class ServiceIn(BaseModel):
    name: str = Field(min_length=2, max_length=80)
    price_minor: int = Field(ge=0, description="Price in paise/cents")

class Service(ServiceIn):
    id: int

_db: dict[int, Service] = {}

@app.get("/health")
def health() -> dict[str, str]:
    return {"status": "ok"}

@app.post("/api/services", response_model=Service, status_code=201)
def create_service(payload: ServiceIn) -> Service:
    sid = len(_db) + 1
    _db[sid] = Service(id=sid, **payload.model_dump())
    return _db[sid]

@app.get("/api/services/{sid}", response_model=Service)
def get_service(sid: int) -> Service:
    if sid not in _db:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=404, detail="Service not found")
    return _db[sid]

8 · Expected output

POST /api/services {"name":"Whitening","price_minor":450000}
  -> 201 {"name":"Whitening","price_minor":450000,"id":1}
GET  /api/services/9 -> 404 {"detail":"Service not found"}
POST with name "A"   -> 422 (validation error list)
9 · Verificationpytest -q passes; /docs lists every endpoint with examples.
10 · Common errorsBusiness logic inside route functions; global mutable state in production; blocking calls inside async def; no versioning of the API.
11 · Security considerationsDisable debug/reload in production; restrict CORS to known origins; never return stack traces to clients.
12 · DocumentationThe generated OpenAPI file is exported into docs/api-specification.md at each release.
13 · Practical assignmentRe-implement the same two endpoints in a second framework (Django REST or Fastify) and write a one-page comparison.
14 · AssessmentExplain which framework you would pick for three client scenarios and why.
15 · Approval gateTech Lead reviews the code and comparison.

Read: FastAPI · Django · Node.js docs

L3.2 · REST API Design

EssentialFree8 h
1 · DefinitionA REST API models business objects as resources with predictable URLs, standard HTTP methods and consistent JSON. Good design covers naming, status codes, pagination, filtering, versioning and idempotency.
2 · Business purposeA predictable API cuts integration time for the frontend, mobile apps and the client's other systems, and keeps maintenance cost low.
3 · Real-world exampleGET /api/v1/orders?status=paid&page=2&page_size=20 lists orders; POST /api/v1/orders creates one; PATCH /api/v1/orders/17 changes it; DELETE cancels it.
4 · PrerequisitesL1.8, L3.1.
5 · Tools & installationPostman, OpenAPI/Swagger, FastAPI /docs.

6 · Step-by-step procedure

  1. List resources as plural nouns (/orders, /orders/{id}/items).
  2. Map operations to methods and status codes (201 create, 204 delete, 404 missing, 409 conflict, 422 validation).
  3. Add pagination (page, page_size with a maximum) and filtering on every list endpoint.
  4. Add an Idempotency-Key header for payment-like POST requests.
  5. Version the path (/api/v1).

7 · Complete example

GET    /api/v1/orders                 200  list (paginated)
POST   /api/v1/orders                 201  create  (Idempotency-Key supported)
GET    /api/v1/orders/{id}            200 | 404
PATCH  /api/v1/orders/{id}            200 | 404 | 409 | 422
DELETE /api/v1/orders/{id}            204 | 404

List response:
{ "items": [ ... ], "page": 2, "page_size": 20, "total": 143 }

8 · Expected output

A table of endpoints with request/response examples and error cases for one module of the sample project.
9 · VerificationA teammate can build the frontend screen from the written spec alone, without reading the backend code.
10 · Common errorsVerbs in URLs (/getOrders); returning 200 for errors; unbounded list endpoints; inconsistent field names (userId vs user_id).
11 · Security considerationsRate-limit auth and expensive endpoints; check ownership on every {id} route (prevents IDOR); never expose internal ids/fields you do not need.
12 · DocumentationComplete the endpoint table in docs/api-specification.md before coding.
13 · Practical assignmentWrite the API specification for the booking system (services, slots, bookings, payments).
14 · AssessmentPeer review another employee's spec using the standard checklist.
15 · Approval gateSpec approved before implementation (this is a mandatory project gate).

Read: OWASP API Security Top 10

L3.3 · Authentication

EssentialFree12 h
1 · DefinitionAuthentication proves who the user is. Common approaches are server-side sessions in an httpOnly cookie, JWT access tokens with short expiry plus refresh tokens, and delegated OAuth 2.0/OpenID Connect sign-in (Google, Microsoft). Passwords are stored only as salted slow hashes (Argon2id or bcrypt).
2 · Business purposeLogin is the front door of every portal, dashboard and SaaS product. A mistake here leads directly to account takeover and data breach.
3 · Real-world exampleA customer portal logs users in with email and password, issues a 15-minute access token and a rotating refresh token in httpOnly cookies, and supports "Sign in with Google" for staff.
4 · PrerequisitesL3.1, L3.2, L1.3.
5 · Tools & installationargon2-cffi, PyJWT (Python); bcrypt/jose (Node); or a managed provider (Auth0, Clerk, Firebase Auth, Cognito, Keycloak) - paid or free by plan, verify current terms.

6 · Step-by-step procedure

  1. Hash passwords with Argon2id; never log or return them.
  2. Verify the password in constant time and return a generic error on failure.
  3. Issue a short-lived token/session; set cookie flags HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax.
  4. Add rate limiting, account lockout/backoff and a password-reset flow with single-use expiring tokens.
  5. Offer MFA for admin accounts.

7 · Complete example

import os, datetime as dt
import jwt                                   # PyJWT
from argon2 import PasswordHasher
from argon2.exceptions import VerifyMismatchError

ph = PasswordHasher()                        # Argon2id defaults
SECRET = os.environ["JWT_SECRET"]            # from environment, never in Git

stored_hash = ph.hash("S3cure-pass!")

def login(password: str, user_id: int, role: str) -> str | None:
    try:
        ph.verify(stored_hash, password)
    except VerifyMismatchError:
        return None                          # same message for wrong user or password
    now = dt.datetime.now(dt.timezone.utc)
    claims = {"sub": str(user_id), "role": role, "iat": now, "exp": now + dt.timedelta(minutes=15)}
    return jwt.encode(claims, SECRET, algorithm="HS256")

token = login("S3cure-pass!", 42, "customer")
print(jwt.decode(token, SECRET, algorithms=["HS256"])["role"])   # customer

8 · Expected output

customer
(login with a wrong password returns None; an expired token raises jwt.ExpiredSignatureError)
9 · VerificationTests prove: wrong password rejected, expired token rejected, tampered token rejected, rate limit triggers after N attempts.
10 · Common errorsStoring plain or fast-hash (MD5/SHA-1) passwords; secrets hard-coded; tokens that never expire; different error messages that reveal whether an email exists; alg not pinned.
11 · Security considerationsOWASP ASVS authentication controls; rotate secrets; invalidate sessions on password change; use HTTPS everywhere; protect against CSRF when using cookies.
12 · DocumentationAuth flow diagram and token lifetimes in docs/security.md.
13 · Practical assignmentBuild register, login, logout, refresh and password-reset endpoints with tests (Project 3).
14 · AssessmentSecurity review - the Tech Lead attempts five common attacks (credential stuffing, token tampering, brute force, replay, CSRF) against your API.
15 · Approval gateAll five attacks fail; Tech Lead signs the security checklist.

Read: OWASP Cheat Sheets - Authentication · OWASP ASVS

L3.4 · Authorisation

EssentialFree6 h
1 · DefinitionAuthorisation decides what an authenticated user may do. Models - RBAC (roles such as admin/staff/customer), ownership checks (a user may edit only their own records) and permissions/policies for finer rules.
2 · Business purposeBroken access control is the number-one web risk (OWASP Top 10). One missing check can let a customer read another customer's invoices.
3 · Real-world exampleA customer calls GET /orders/17. The API loads the order and returns 404 unless order.customer_id equals the caller's id; staff may read any order but not delete it; only admin may delete.
4 · PrerequisitesL3.3.
5 · Tools & installationFramework dependency/middleware system (FastAPI Depends, Django permissions, Nest guards); optional policy engines (Casbin, OPA).

6 · Step-by-step procedure

  1. Write an access matrix - role by action by resource.
  2. Implement authentication once as a dependency; implement role and ownership checks as reusable functions.
  3. Deny by default; require an explicit allow.
  4. Test the matrix - every cell has an automated test.

7 · Complete example

from fastapi import Depends, HTTPException

def require_role(*allowed: str):
    def checker(user=Depends(current_user)):          # current_user validates the token
        if user.role not in allowed:
            raise HTTPException(status_code=403, detail="Forbidden")
        return user
    return checker

@app.delete("/api/v1/orders/{oid}", status_code=204)
def delete_order(oid: int, user=Depends(require_role("admin"))):
    ...

@app.get("/api/v1/orders/{oid}")
def get_order(oid: int, user=Depends(current_user)):
    order = repo.get_order(oid)
    if order is None or (user.role == "customer" and order.customer_id != user.id):
        raise HTTPException(status_code=404)           # do not reveal that it exists
    return order

8 · Expected output

customer reads own order      -> 200
customer reads another's      -> 404
staff deletes order           -> 403
admin deletes order           -> 204
9 · VerificationThe access-matrix test suite passes and is run in CI.
10 · Common errorsChecking permissions only in the frontend; trusting a role field sent by the client; forgetting list endpoints (leaking other users' rows through filters).
11 · Security considerationsEnforce on the server, deny by default, log access-denied events, re-check on every request.
12 · DocumentationAccess matrix table in docs/security.md.
13 · Practical assignmentAdd roles and ownership rules to the Project 3 application and write the matrix tests.
14 · AssessmentGiven a codebase with three planted IDOR bugs, find and fix them.
15 · Approval gateTech Lead review of the access matrix and tests.

Read: OWASP Top 10

L3.5 · Business Logic and Service Layer

EssentialFree8 h
1 · DefinitionBusiness logic is the client's rules turned into code - pricing, discounts, stock, availability, approvals. The service layer keeps those rules in plain, testable functions separate from HTTP routes and database queries.
2 · Business purposeRules change often (offers, tax, policies). When logic is isolated and tested, changes are quick and safe, and the client's money is calculated correctly.
3 · Real-world examplecreate_booking() checks the slot is free, applies the member discount, creates the booking and the payment intent in one transaction, and returns the result - routes only translate HTTP to and from this function.
4 · PrerequisitesL3.2, L4.1 (concepts).
5 · Tools & installationPytest/Jest unit tests; a clear folder structure (routes, services, repositories).

6 · Step-by-step procedure

  1. Write the rule in plain language with examples.
  2. Implement it as a pure function where possible (inputs in, result out).
  3. Keep money in integer minor units and use Decimal for rate maths.
  4. Write unit tests from the examples first, including edge cases (zero, negative, boundaries).
  5. Call the service from the route; keep the route thin.

7 · Complete example

from decimal import Decimal, ROUND_HALF_UP

def price_with_gst(net_minor: int, gst_percent: Decimal = Decimal("18")) -> dict[str, int]:
    """Return net, tax and gross in minor units (paise). Rounds half up per line."""
    tax = (Decimal(net_minor) * gst_percent / Decimal(100)).quantize(Decimal("1"), rounding=ROUND_HALF_UP)
    return {"net": net_minor, "tax": int(tax), "gross": net_minor + int(tax)}

assert price_with_gst(100_000) == {"net": 100000, "tax": 18000, "gross": 118000}
assert price_with_gst(10_001)["tax"] == 1800   # 1800.18 rounds to 1800

8 · Expected output

Both assertions pass silently; a failing rule raises `AssertionError` with the mismatch.
9 · VerificationUnit tests cover normal, boundary and invalid inputs; mutation of a rule makes a test fail.
10 · Common errorsRules duplicated in frontend and backend; floating-point money; rounding differences between invoice and ledger; business logic hidden in SQL triggers nobody documents.
11 · Security considerationsNever trust prices or totals from the client; recompute on the server; log who changed rule configuration.
12 · DocumentationBusiness rules glossary with examples in docs/requirements.md.
13 · Practical assignmentImplement discount, coupon and tax rules for the e-commerce prototype with at least 25 unit tests.
14 · AssessmentClient-style change request - "Add a 10% loyalty discount above Rs 5,000 but not with coupons". Implement and test in 90 minutes.
15 · Approval gateTests green; Tech Lead reviews rule coverage.

L3.6 · Input Validation

EssentialFree5 h
1 · DefinitionValidation ensures every value entering the system has the right type, length, range and format before it is used. Validate at the edge (request models), then enforce again in the database with constraints.
2 · Business purposeMost injection, corruption and crash bugs start with unvalidated input. Validation also gives users clear, fast error messages.
3 · Real-world exampleA registration endpoint rejects an email without @, a 3-character password, a 5,000-character name and an unknown role value - each with a precise message.
4 · PrerequisitesL3.1.
5 · Tools & installationPydantic (Python), Zod/Valibot (TypeScript), Django forms/serializers, database CHECK/UNIQUE/NOT NULL.

6 · Step-by-step procedure

  1. Define a request model for every endpoint (no raw dicts).
  2. Set min/max lengths, ranges, patterns and enums; use allow-lists, not block-lists.
  3. Normalise (trim, lowercase email) before validating uniqueness.
  4. Reject unknown fields where mass-assignment is a risk.
  5. Mirror critical rules as database constraints.

7 · Complete example

from pydantic import BaseModel, EmailStr, Field, ConfigDict
from typing import Literal

class RegisterIn(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid", str_strip_whitespace=True)
    email: EmailStr
    password: str = Field(min_length=10, max_length=128)
    name: str = Field(min_length=2, max_length=80)
    role: Literal["customer"] = "customer"        # clients can never choose admin

8 · Expected output

422 Unprocessable Entity
{"detail":[{"loc":["body","password"],"msg":"String should have at least 10 characters", ...}]}
9 · VerificationA table-driven test of valid and invalid payloads passes, including very long strings and unexpected fields.
10 · Common errorsValidating only in the browser; accepting any JSON object and saving it; trusting file names or MIME types; regexes that cause catastrophic backtracking.
11 · Security considerationsParameterised queries for SQL; output-encode on rendering; validate file uploads (L3.8); apply size limits at the proxy and framework.
12 · DocumentationValidation rules are the single source in the request models and appear in the API spec.
13 · Practical assignmentWrite validation tests with at least 30 cases for the registration and booking endpoints.
14 · AssessmentFuzz your own API with 20 malicious payloads (long strings, SQL fragments, unicode, nulls) and record the results.
15 · Approval gateNo 500 errors from any fuzz case; mentor sign-off.

Read: OWASP Input Validation Cheat Sheet

L3.7 · Error Handling and Logging Contracts

EssentialFree5 h
1 · DefinitionError handling means every failure produces a safe, consistent response for the user and a detailed log record for the team. Distinguish client errors (4xx - fixable by the caller) from server errors (5xx - our fault).
2 · Business purposeClients judge a product by how it fails. Clear messages reduce support calls; correlation ids let us find the cause in minutes.
3 · Real-world exampleA payment timeout returns 502 with {error:{code:'PAYMENT_UNAVAILABLE', message:'Please try again', request_id:'a1b2'}} while the log holds the full exception and the gateway response.
4 · PrerequisitesL3.1, L3.6.
5 · Tools & installationFramework exception handlers, structured logger (structlog, pino), Sentry (free tier - check current limits).

6 · Step-by-step procedure

  1. Define one error format used by every endpoint.
  2. Add global handlers for validation, not-found, domain and unexpected errors.
  3. Generate a request id per call, return it in the response header and put it in every log line.
  4. Never leak internals - SQL, file paths, stack traces - to the client.
  5. Add retries with limits only for safe, idempotent calls.

7 · Complete example

import logging, uuid
from fastapi import Request
from fastapi.responses import JSONResponse

log = logging.getLogger("api")

@app.middleware("http")
async def request_id(request: Request, call_next):
    request.state.rid = request.headers.get("x-request-id", uuid.uuid4().hex[:12])
    response = await call_next(request)
    response.headers["x-request-id"] = request.state.rid
    return response

@app.exception_handler(Exception)
async def unhandled(request: Request, exc: Exception):
    log.exception("unhandled error rid=%s path=%s", request.state.rid, request.url.path)
    return JSONResponse(status_code=500, content={"error": {"code": "INTERNAL", "message": "Something went wrong.", "request_id": request.state.rid}})

8 · Expected output

HTTP/1.1 500
x-request-id: 3f9a2c1b7d04
{"error":{"code":"INTERNAL","message":"Something went wrong.","request_id":"3f9a2c1b7d04"}}
9 · VerificationForce an error in a test; the response is safe and the log line carries the same request id.
10 · Common errorsSwallowing exceptions (except: pass); returning 200 with an error; logging secrets or full card/personal data; inconsistent error shapes.
11 · Security considerationsError responses must not reveal stack traces, queries or user existence; mask personal data in logs.
12 · DocumentationError code catalogue in docs/api-specification.md.
13 · Practical assignmentAdd global error handling, request ids and structured logs to the Project 3 API.
14 · AssessmentGiven an incident description and a request id, find the root cause from logs alone.
15 · Approval gateTech Lead review.

L3.8 · File Uploads

EssentialFree6 h
1 · DefinitionA file upload lets users send files (images, PDFs, CSVs) to the server. Safe handling needs size limits, type verification by content, random storage names, private storage and, for large files, direct-to-storage uploads with pre-signed URLs.
2 · Business purposeUpload features (profile pictures, KYC documents, invoices) are a frequent route for malware, storage abuse and data leaks.
3 · Real-world exampleA user uploads a PDF invoice. The API checks size and real file type, stores it in a private bucket under a random key, saves only the key in the database and serves it later through a short-lived signed link.
4 · PrerequisitesL3.6.
5 · Tools & installationFastAPI UploadFile/python-multipart; python-magic or filetype; S3-compatible object storage (AWS S3, Cloudflare R2, Azure Blob - check current pricing); optional antivirus scanning (ClamAV).

6 · Step-by-step procedure

  1. Set a maximum size at the proxy (e.g. Nginx client_max_body_size) and in the app.
  2. Allow-list extensions and verify the real content type from the file bytes.
  3. Generate a random name; never use the client's file name in a path.
  4. Store outside the web root or in a private bucket; scan if the data is untrusted.
  5. Serve through authenticated, expiring links.

7 · Complete example

import secrets, pathlib
from fastapi import UploadFile, HTTPException

ALLOWED = {"image/jpeg": ".jpg", "image/png": ".png", "application/pdf": ".pdf"}
MAX_BYTES = 5 * 1024 * 1024
STORE = pathlib.Path("/var/app/uploads")        # private folder, not served by Nginx

async def save_upload(file: UploadFile) -> str:
    data = await file.read(MAX_BYTES + 1)
    if len(data) > MAX_BYTES:
        raise HTTPException(413, "File too large (max 5 MB)")
    kind = sniff_mime(data)                      # inspect bytes, e.g. with python-magic
    if kind not in ALLOWED:
        raise HTTPException(415, "Unsupported file type")
    key = secrets.token_hex(16) + ALLOWED[kind]
    (STORE / key).write_bytes(data)
    return key

8 · Expected output

5.2 MB file -> 413 File too large
renamed .exe -> 415 Unsupported file type
valid PDF   -> 201 {"file_key":"9c1e...b7.pdf"}
9 · VerificationTests upload an oversized file, a disguised executable, a path-traversal name (../../x) and a valid file; only the last succeeds.
10 · Common errorsTrusting Content-Type or the extension; saving with the original name; keeping uploads inside the public folder; reading huge files fully into memory.
11 · Security considerationsOWASP file-upload guidance - allow-list, random names, private storage, scanning, no execution rights on the upload folder, SVG treated as active content.
12 · DocumentationAllowed types, limits and storage location in docs/security.md.
13 · Practical assignmentAdd avatar upload and invoice PDF upload with signed download links to Project 4.
14 · AssessmentAttack your own upload endpoint with five malicious files and report the results.
15 · Approval gateAll malicious uploads rejected; Tech Lead sign-off.

L3.9 · Email Integration

EssentialPaid6 h
1 · DefinitionTransactional email is automated mail triggered by an action - verification, receipt, password reset. It is sent through SMTP or a provider API (Amazon SES, SendGrid, Mailgun, Postmark, Resend, Microsoft 365). Deliverability depends on SPF, DKIM and DMARC DNS records.
2 · Business purposePassword resets, booking confirmations and invoices must reach the inbox. Misconfigured domains send client emails to spam or let attackers spoof the client's brand.
3 · Real-world exampleAfter booking, the system queues a confirmation email with an .ics calendar attachment; a worker sends it and records the provider's message id.
4 · PrerequisitesL3.5, L1.4.
5 · Tools & installationProvider SDK/SMTP, a template engine (Jinja2, React Email, MJML), a background queue (Celery, RQ, BullMQ) and a local test inbox (Mailpit, free).

6 · Step-by-step procedure

  1. Choose a provider and read its current pricing and limits on the official site.
  2. Verify the sending domain; add the SPF, DKIM and DMARC records it provides.
  3. Build HTML + plain-text templates with variables; never put secrets in links without expiry.
  4. Send through a queue with retries; record status and provider message id.
  5. Test locally with Mailpit before using the real provider.

7 · Complete example

import smtplib
from email.message import EmailMessage

def send_reset(to: str, link: str) -> None:
    msg = EmailMessage()
    msg["From"], msg["To"], msg["Subject"] = "no-reply@clientdomain.com", to, "Reset your password"
    msg.set_content(f"Use this link within 30 minutes:\n{link}\nIf you did not ask, ignore this email.")
    with smtplib.SMTP("localhost", 1025) as s:     # Mailpit in development
        s.send_message(msg)

8 · Expected output

The message appears in the Mailpit web UI at `http://localhost:8025`; in production the same call goes to the provider with credentials from environment variables.
9 · VerificationAn email to a Gmail test account passes SPF, DKIM and DMARC (view message headers: Authentication-Results).
10 · Common errorsSending from an unverified domain; no plain-text part; long-lived reset links; sending synchronously inside the request; no unsubscribe on marketing mail.
11 · Security considerationsReset tokens are random, single-use and expire; do not reveal whether an email is registered; protect provider API keys; follow anti-spam law (consent, unsubscribe).
12 · DocumentationEmail types, templates, sender domains and DNS records in docs/deployment.md.
13 · Practical assignmentImplement verification, reset and booking-confirmation emails with a queue and tests.
14 · AssessmentDiagnose three failure cases (SPF fail, DKIM missing, link expired) from headers and logs.
15 · Approval gateLevel 3 completion review - modules signed; Project 3 authentication app accepted.

Read: FastAPI · OWASP

Level 4 - Database Engineering (about 3 weeks)

Goal: design, build, query, tune, migrate and back up relational databases.

L4.1 · PostgreSQL and MySQL - Choosing and Installing

EssentialFree5 h
1 · DefinitionPostgreSQL and MySQL/MariaDB are open-source relational database servers. PostgreSQL has the richest feature set (JSONB, advanced indexes, strong standards compliance, row-level security). MySQL/MariaDB is widely supported by hosting panels and WordPress/WooCommerce.
2 · Business purposeThe database engine is hard to change later. We default to PostgreSQL for custom applications and use MySQL/MariaDB when the platform requires it (WordPress, WooCommerce, some legacy systems).
3 · Real-world exampleA custom SaaS platform uses PostgreSQL on a managed service. A WooCommerce shop keeps MySQL because the plugin ecosystem expects it.
4 · PrerequisitesL1.7.
5 · Tools & installationPostgreSQL (free, open source), MySQL Community Edition / MariaDB (free), Docker, psql, DBeaver or pgAdmin (free). Managed services (AWS RDS, Azure Database, Cloud SQL, Supabase, Neon, PlanetScale) are paid or have limited free tiers - check each vendor's current pricing.

6 · Step-by-step procedure

  1. Run PostgreSQL in Docker for development (command below).
  2. Connect with psql, create a database and an application user with limited rights.
  3. Repeat for MySQL/MariaDB and list three syntax differences you meet.
  4. Write a one-page decision note - when PostgreSQL, when MySQL, when a managed service.

7 · Complete example

docker run --name pg-dev -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=devonly -p 5432:5432 -d postgres:16
psql "postgresql://postgres:devonly@localhost:5432/postgres" -c "CREATE DATABASE clinic;"
psql "postgresql://postgres:devonly@localhost:5432/clinic" <<'SQL'
CREATE ROLE app_user LOGIN PASSWORD 'change-me-dev';
GRANT CONNECT ON DATABASE clinic TO app_user;
SQL

8 · Expected output

CREATE DATABASE
CREATE ROLE
GRANT
9 · Verificationpsql -c "SELECT version();" prints the server version; app_user cannot create or drop databases.
10 · Common errorsUsing the postgres superuser in the application; exposing port 5432 publicly; confusing users (application table) with database roles; default passwords left in place.
11 · Security considerationsDedicated least-privilege application role; strong secrets from a secret store; TLS to the database; private network only; automated patching.
12 · DocumentationDatabase section of docs/architecture.md - engine, version, hosting, access method.
13 · Practical assignmentInstall both engines locally and load the same 3-table schema into each.
14 · AssessmentExplain three real differences (types, auto-increment/identity, quoting, JSON handling).
15 · Approval gateMentor sign-off.

Read: PostgreSQL docs · MySQL reference

L4.2 · Database Design and Normalisation

EssentialFree8 h
1 · DefinitionDatabase design turns business information into tables, columns, keys and constraints. Normalisation removes duplication - 1NF (atomic values), 2NF (no partial dependency), 3NF (no transitive dependency) - so each fact is stored once.
2 · Business purposeA good design makes reports accurate, updates safe and growth cheap. A poor one produces duplicate customers, wrong totals and expensive rewrites.
3 · Real-world exampleInstead of repeating the customer's address on every order row, store the address once in customers and reference it by customer_id.
4 · PrerequisitesL1.7, L4.1.
5 · Tools & installationdbdiagram.io, draw.io, pgModeler or DBeaver ER view; SQL DDL.

6 · Step-by-step procedure

  1. Interview the client and list nouns (entities) and verbs (relationships).
  2. Choose primary keys; add natural unique keys (email, SKU) as UNIQUE constraints.
  3. Normalise to 3NF; denormalise only with a measured reason.
  4. Add NOT NULL, CHECK, UNIQUE and FOREIGN KEY constraints.
  5. Add audit columns (created_at, updated_at) and soft-delete only where required.

7 · Complete example

CREATE TABLE services (
  id           BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  name         VARCHAR(80)  NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  duration_min INTEGER      NOT NULL CHECK (duration_min BETWEEN 5 AND 480),
  price_minor  INTEGER      NOT NULL CHECK (price_minor >= 0),
  active       BOOLEAN      NOT NULL DEFAULT TRUE,
  created_at   TIMESTAMPTZ  NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

8 · Expected output

`CREATE TABLE`. Inserting a negative price or a 0-minute service fails with a CHECK-constraint violation.
9 · VerificationTry to insert invalid rows - the database itself rejects them.
10 · Common errorsMoney as FLOAT; no foreign keys "for speed"; one giant table; storing lists in a text column; EAV (entity-attribute-value) tables for everything.
11 · Security considerationsStore only data you need; classify personal data; plan encryption for sensitive columns and retention periods; never store card numbers (use the gateway's tokens).
12 · DocumentationER diagram + data dictionary (table, column, type, meaning) in docs/database-design.md.
13 · Practical assignmentDesign the schema for the booking system (Project 4) with at least 6 tables and a data dictionary.
14 · AssessmentReview a flawed schema and list 8 problems with fixes.
15 · Approval gateDesign review by Tech Lead - mandatory project gate before implementation.

L4.3 · Relationships and Keys

EssentialFree5 h
1 · DefinitionRelationships link tables: one-to-many (customer -> orders), many-to-many via a junction table (students <-> courses) and one-to-one. Foreign keys make the database enforce them; ON DELETE rules define what happens to children.
2 · Business purposeCorrect relationships keep data consistent without relying on every developer to remember a rule.
3 · Real-world exampleorder_items(order_id, product_id, qty) links orders to products; deleting an order removes its items (ON DELETE CASCADE), but deleting a product that was ever sold is blocked (RESTRICT).
4 · PrerequisitesL4.2.
5 · Tools & installationpsql, DBeaver, ER diagram tool.

6 · Step-by-step procedure

  1. For each relationship decide cardinality and whether the child can exist without the parent.
  2. Create foreign keys with an explicit ON DELETE rule.
  3. Create a junction table with a composite primary key for many-to-many.
  4. Index foreign-key columns used in joins.

7 · Complete example

CREATE TABLE orders (
  id BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT
);
CREATE TABLE order_items (
  order_id   BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES orders(id)   ON DELETE CASCADE,
  product_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES products(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT,
  qty        INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (qty > 0),
  unit_price_minor INTEGER NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (order_id, product_id)
);
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer ON orders(customer_id);

8 · Expected output
