Deleting a customer with orders fails with a foreign-key error; deleting an order also deletes its items.
9 · VerificationA script inserts orphan rows and attempts risky deletes - all are blocked or cascade as documented.
10 · Common errorsMissing index on the foreign key; CASCADE chains that delete too much; many-to-many modelled as a comma list.
11 · Security considerationsON DELETE CASCADE can erase large volumes - restrict it to true ownership relations and require backups before bulk deletes.
12 · DocumentationRelationship table (parent, child, cardinality, delete rule) in docs/database-design.md.
13 · Practical assignmentAdd junction tables and rules for tags, categories and product variants to the e-commerce schema.
14 · AssessmentExplain the effect of each ON DELETE option with a live demo.
15 · Approval gateMentor sign-off.

L4.4 · SQL

EssentialFree14 h
1 · DefinitionSQL (Structured Query Language) reads and changes relational data - SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, JOIN, GROUP BY, HAVING, subqueries and CTEs (WITH), and window functions.
2 · Business purposeEvery report, dashboard and data fix depends on SQL. Fluent SQL turns a client's vague question ("who are my best customers?") into an answer in minutes.
3 · Real-world exampleTop customers by revenue in the last 90 days is one query joining customers, orders and order items.
4 · PrerequisitesL4.2, L4.3.
5 · Tools & installationpsql, DBeaver; sample dataset (pagila / the training schema).

6 · Step-by-step procedure

  1. Practise SELECT with WHERE, ORDER BY, LIMIT.
  2. Practise INNER and LEFT JOIN; explain the difference with row counts.
  3. Aggregate with GROUP BY and HAVING.
  4. Write a CTE and a window function (RANK() OVER).
  5. Always use parameters, never string concatenation, from application code.

7 · Complete example

WITH spend AS (
  SELECT c.id, c.name, SUM(oi.qty * oi.unit_price_minor) AS total_minor
  FROM customers c
  JOIN orders o       ON o.customer_id = c.id
  JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id   = o.id
  WHERE o.created_at >= now() - INTERVAL '90 days'
  GROUP BY c.id, c.name
)
SELECT name, total_minor, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY total_minor DESC) AS rnk
FROM spend
ORDER BY rnk
LIMIT 10;

8 · Expected output

name    | total_minor | rnk
--------+-------------+-----
Asha    |      459000 |   1
Karthik |      312500 |   2
9 · VerificationCompare the query result to a manual total for one customer; run EXPLAIN and confirm no unexpected full scans on large tables.
10 · Common errorsSELECT * in production code; missing JOIN condition (cartesian product); NOT IN with NULLs; UPDATE or DELETE without WHERE.
11 · Security considerationsSQL injection is prevented only by parameterised queries; run UPDATE/DELETE first as SELECT to see the rows; use a transaction for data fixes.
12 · DocumentationKeep reusable reporting queries in database/queries/ with a comment explaining intent.
13 · Practical assignmentAnswer 20 business questions with SQL against the training database.
14 · AssessmentTimed SQL test (10 queries in 60 minutes).
15 · Approval gateScore at least 80%.

Read: PostgreSQL tutorial

L4.5 · Indexes and Query Performance

EssentialFree6 h
1 · DefinitionAn index is an extra data structure (usually a B-tree) that lets the database find rows without scanning the whole table. EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) shows the query plan and actual timings.
2 · Business purposeIndexes are the cheapest performance win - and over-indexing slows writes and wastes storage. Slow queries are a top cause of timeouts under load.
3 · Real-world exampleSearching orders by customer_id on a 5-million-row table drops from seconds to milliseconds after adding an index on that column.
4 · PrerequisitesL4.4.
5 · Tools & installationEXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS), pg_stat_statements, pgAdmin/DBeaver.

6 · Step-by-step procedure

  1. Generate a large test table (1 million rows) and run a filtered query.
  2. Read the plan - note Seq Scan and its time.
  3. Create an index on the filter column and re-run - note Index Scan.
  4. Add a composite index for a common filter + sort and observe the plan.
  5. Drop indexes that are never used.

7 · Complete example

CREATE TABLE big_orders AS
SELECT g AS id, (random()*100000)::int AS customer_id, now() - (g || ' minutes')::interval AS created_at
FROM generate_series(1, 1000000) g;

EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) SELECT * FROM big_orders WHERE customer_id = 4242;
CREATE INDEX idx_big_orders_customer ON big_orders (customer_id, created_at DESC);
ANALYZE big_orders;
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) SELECT * FROM big_orders WHERE customer_id = 4242 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 5;

8 · Expected output

Before: Seq Scan on big_orders ... Execution Time: ~60-150 ms (hardware dependent)
After : Index Scan using idx_big_orders_customer ... Execution Time: < 1 ms
9 · VerificationThe plan changes from Seq Scan to Index Scan and execution time drops by an order of magnitude.
10 · Common errorsIndexing every column; function on the indexed column in WHERE (lower(email) needs an expression index); stale statistics; leading wildcard LIKE '%x'.
11 · Security considerationsIndexes copy data - they inherit the sensitivity of the column; do not index unneeded personal data.
12 · DocumentationRecord each non-obvious index and the query it serves in docs/database-design.md.
13 · Practical assignmentTune three slow queries provided by the mentor and write before/after evidence.
14 · AssessmentExplain a given query plan line by line.
15 · Approval gateEvidence reviewed by Tech Lead.

L4.6 · Transactions and Concurrency

EssentialFree6 h
1 · DefinitionA transaction groups statements so they all succeed or all fail (ACID - atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability). Isolation levels and row locks control what concurrent users see and prevent double-booking.
2 · Business purposePayments, stock and bookings must never end half-done or be sold twice. Transactions are how the database guarantees that.
3 · Real-world exampleBooking the last 10:00 slot: two customers click at the same moment. A transaction with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE lets only one succeed.
4 · PrerequisitesL4.4.
5 · Tools & installationpsql with two terminals; the application's DB driver/ORM transaction API.

6 · Step-by-step procedure

  1. Run BEGIN; ... ROLLBACK; and COMMIT; in psql and observe visibility from a second session.
  2. Reproduce a double-booking race with two sessions.
  3. Fix it with FOR UPDATE or a UNIQUE constraint on (slot, resource).
  4. Keep transactions short; never wait for user input or an external API inside one.

7 · Complete example

BEGIN;
SELECT id FROM slots WHERE id = 77 AND booked = FALSE FOR UPDATE;   -- locks the row
UPDATE slots SET booked = TRUE WHERE id = 77;
INSERT INTO bookings (slot_id, user_id) VALUES (77, 42);
COMMIT;
-- Safety net: ALTER TABLE bookings ADD CONSTRAINT uq_slot UNIQUE (slot_id);

8 · Expected output

Two sessions run concurrently: one commits, the other either waits and finds `booked = TRUE`, or fails with a unique violation - never both succeed.
9 · VerificationA concurrency test with 20 parallel requests creates exactly one booking.
10 · Common errorsAuto-commit per statement for multi-step operations; long transactions holding locks; deadlocks from inconsistent lock order; swallowing the error after a failed statement.
11 · Security considerationsNever leave a transaction open in a failing connection pool; log failed financial transactions for audit.
12 · DocumentationList which operations are transactional in docs/architecture.md.
13 · Practical assignmentImplement and test race-safe booking and stock decrement.
14 · AssessmentExplain READ COMMITTED vs REPEATABLE READ with an example each.
15 · Approval gateConcurrency tests green.

L4.7 · Migrations and Seed Data

EssentialFree6 h
1 · DefinitionA migration is a versioned, reviewable script that changes the database structure from one state to the next (Alembic, Django migrations, Prisma Migrate, Flyway, Knex). Seeds load reference or demo data.
2 · Business purposeMigrations make every environment identical and reproducible, and let us deploy schema changes safely and roll them back.
3 · Real-world exampleRelease 1.3 adds a phone column - the migration runs in staging first, then in production, and the same file is in Git history.
4 · PrerequisitesL4.2, L5.1 (Git).
5 · Tools & installationAlembic (SQLAlchemy), Django migrations, Prisma Migrate or Flyway; database/migrations/ and database/seeds/ folders.

6 · Step-by-step procedure

  1. Never edit the schema by hand in staging or production.
  2. Generate a migration, read it, and test upgrade and downgrade on a copy of production-like data.
  3. Use the expand-contract pattern for risky changes (add nullable column, backfill, switch code, then add NOT NULL).
  4. Run migrations in CI and as a controlled deploy step.
  5. Keep seeds idempotent (safe to run twice) and free of real personal data.

7 · Complete example

alembic revision --autogenerate -m "add phone to customers"
alembic upgrade head          # apply
alembic downgrade -1          # prove the rollback works
alembic current               # show the version in this environment

8 · Expected output

INFO  Running upgrade 7a1c... -> b92e..., add phone to customers
INFO  Running downgrade b92e... -> 7a1c..., add phone to customers
9 · VerificationA fresh database built only from migrations equals the one in staging (schema diff is empty).
10 · Common errorsEditing an already-applied migration; migrations that lock a big table for minutes; data changes mixed with schema changes; no downgrade plan.
11 · Security considerationsMigration credentials differ from application credentials; seeds contain no real customers or passwords.
12 · DocumentationMigration policy and the release runbook in docs/deployment.md.
13 · Practical assignmentCreate five migrations for Project 4, including one using expand-contract.
14 · AssessmentPlan the safest way to rename a column on a live table.
15 · Approval gateTech Lead reviews migrations.

L4.8 · Backup and Recovery

EssentialFree6 h
1 · DefinitionA backup is a restorable copy of data. Key terms - RPO (how much data loss is acceptable) and RTO (how long recovery may take). Methods include logical dumps (pg_dump), physical/base backups with WAL archiving for point-in-time recovery, and managed-service snapshots.
2 · Business purposeA backup that has never been restored is only a hope. Data loss from deletion, ransomware or a bad migration is an existential risk for the client.
3 · Real-world exampleThe client's RPO is 15 minutes and RTO is 1 hour. We use managed PITR snapshots plus a nightly dump copied to a separate account, and test a restore every quarter.
4 · PrerequisitesL4.1, L4.7.
5 · Tools & installationpg_dump, pg_restore, mysqldump, cloud snapshots, object storage in a separate account/region, cron or scheduler.

6 · Step-by-step procedure

  1. Agree RPO and RTO with the client in writing.
  2. Automate backups; encrypt them and store a copy off the primary account/region.
  3. Restore into a scratch database and run verification queries.
  4. Record the restore time and compare it to the RTO.
  5. Alert when a backup fails or is older than expected.

7 · Complete example

pg_dump --format=custom --file=clinic_$(date +%F).dump "$DATABASE_URL"
createdb clinic_restore_test
pg_restore --dbname=clinic_restore_test --no-owner clinic_$(date +%F).dump
psql clinic_restore_test -c "SELECT count(*) FROM bookings;"

8 · Expected output

A row count matching production at backup time, and a log line `restore completed in 4m12s`.
9 · VerificationA documented restore test exists for every project; the latest is under 90 days old.
10 · Common errorsBackups stored on the same server; never restoring; no encryption; forgetting uploaded files and configuration; assuming the host backs up automatically.
11 · Security considerationsBackups contain personal data - encrypt, restrict access, set retention and deletion rules; keep one immutable or offline copy.
12 · DocumentationBackup and restore runbook in docs/deployment.md; restore-test log in qa/.
13 · Practical assignmentWrite and execute a backup + restore drill for the Project 4 database.
14 · AssessmentGiven a "table dropped by mistake at 14:05" scenario, perform the recovery within the RTO.
15 · Approval gateLevel 4 completion review - modules signed; Project 4 CRUD application accepted with restore evidence.

Read: PostgreSQL - Backup and Restore

Level 5 - Professional Engineering (about 4 weeks)

Goal: work like a professional - version control, review, testing, containers, pipelines, cloud, observability and security.

L5.1 · Git

EssentialFree8 h
1 · DefinitionGit is a distributed version-control system. It records snapshots (commits) of the project, lets many people work in parallel on branches, and can restore any earlier state.
2 · Business purposeGit is the safety net and the audit trail of every client project - who changed what, why, and how to undo it. No code is delivered without it.
3 · Real-world exampleA developer breaks the checkout page at 5 pm. git revert restores the last good behaviour in a minute, and the history shows exactly which change caused it.
4 · PrerequisitesLevel 2 started.
5 · Tools & installationGit (free), VS Code Source Control, git config with company email, SSH key (ed25519).

6 · Step-by-step procedure

  1. Install Git and set user.name and user.email.
  2. Create a repository; make small commits with clear messages.
  3. Create a feature branch, commit, and merge or rebase back.
  4. Resolve a deliberate merge conflict.
  5. Undo safely - git restore, git revert, and know why git reset --hard is dangerous.

7 · Complete example

git config --global user.name "Your Name"
git config --global user.email "you@company.com"
git init demo && cd demo
echo "# Demo" > README.md && git add README.md && git commit -m "docs: add README"
git switch -c feature/contact-form
echo "form" > form.html && git add . && git commit -m "feat(form): add contact form markup"
git switch main && git merge --no-ff feature/contact-form
git log --oneline --graph

8 · Expected output

*   a1b2c3d (HEAD -> main) Merge branch 'feature/contact-form'
|\
| * 9f8e7d6 feat(form): add contact form markup
|/
* 3c4d5e6 docs: add README
9 · VerificationThe graph shows your branch and merge; git status is clean.
10 · Common errorsCommitting secrets or node_modules; huge commits mixing unrelated changes; force-pushing shared branches; working directly on main.
11 · Security considerationsNever commit credentials (see .gitignore and secret scanning); if a secret is committed, rotate it immediately - deleting the commit is not enough.
12 · DocumentationCONTRIBUTING.md explains branch names, commit format and PR rules (Section 6).
13 · Practical assignmentComplete a 20-step Git lab - branch, merge, conflict, revert, tag, cherry-pick.
14 · AssessmentLive demo - recover a "lost" commit using git reflog.
15 · Approval gateMentor sign-off.

Read: Pro Git (free book) · GitHub Docs

L5.2 · GitHub

EssentialFree6 h
1 · DefinitionGitHub hosts Git repositories and adds collaboration - pull requests, issues, projects, Actions (CI/CD), branch protection, code owners, secret scanning and Dependabot. Plans and limits change - confirm on the GitHub pricing page.
2 · Business purposeGitHub is where work is reviewed, tracked and automatically tested. The company organisation holds all client code; personal accounts are never used for client work.
3 · Real-world exampleA pull request changes the pricing rule; two checks run (tests, lint), the Tech Lead reviews, and only then can it merge into main.
4 · PrerequisitesL5.1.
5 · Tools & installationGitHub organisation account with 2FA, GitHub CLI gh, SSH keys, branch protection rules.

6 · Step-by-step procedure

  1. Enable 2FA and add your SSH key.
  2. Create a repository in the company organisation from the template.
  3. Protect main - require pull request, 1 approval, passing checks, no force push.
  4. Open an issue, branch from it, open a PR that links it (Closes #12).
  5. Enable secret scanning and Dependabot alerts.

7 · Complete example

ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "you@company.com"
gh auth login
gh repo create vel-org/client-project --private --template vel-org/web-project-template
git switch -c feat/12-booking-form
git push -u origin feat/12-booking-form
gh pr create --fill --reviewer techlead --body "Closes #12"

8 · Expected output

A PR URL is printed; GitHub shows the checks running and the reviewer requested.
9 · VerificationPushing directly to main is rejected; the PR cannot be merged until the checks pass.
10 · Common errorsCommitting as a personal account; no branch protection; giant PRs; ignoring failed checks; using personal tokens in CI.
11 · Security considerationsUse fine-grained or app tokens; store secrets only in GitHub Secrets/Environments; require signed-off reviews for production workflows.
12 · DocumentationRepository README.md, CODEOWNERS, .github/pull_request_template.md.
13 · Practical assignmentSet up a complete repository with protection rules and a PR template for Project 3.
14 · AssessmentReview a sample PR with three planted problems.
15 · Approval gateTech Lead verifies repository settings against the checklist.

L5.3 · VS Code

EssentialFree3 h
1 · DefinitionVisual Studio Code is a free, extensible code editor with integrated terminal, debugger, Git and extensions. A shared workspace configuration keeps formatting and tools identical across the team.
2 · Business purposeA consistent editor setup removes "works on my machine" formatting noise, speeds up debugging and enforces standards automatically on save.
3 · Real-world examplePrettier and ESLint run on save, so every pull request has the same style without review comments about spacing.
4 · PrerequisitesNone.
5 · Tools & installationVS Code; extensions - ESLint, Prettier, GitLens (optional), Docker, REST Client or Thunder Client, Playwright Test, Python, Error Lens.

6 · Step-by-step procedure

  1. Install VS Code and the company extension pack (listed in .vscode/extensions.json).
  2. Commit .vscode/settings.json with format-on-save.
  3. Learn five shortcuts - command palette, quick open, multi-cursor, go to definition, rename symbol.
  4. Debug a Node or Python program with a breakpoint through launch.json.

7 · Complete example

{
  "editor.formatOnSave": true,
  "editor.defaultFormatter": "esbenp.prettier-vscode",
  "editor.codeActionsOnSave": { "source.fixAll.eslint": "explicit" },
  "files.trimTrailingWhitespace": true,
  "files.insertFinalNewline": true
}

8 · Expected output

Saving a messy file reformats it and fixes lint issues automatically.
9 · VerificationAnother team member opens the project and gets identical formatting with no manual setup.
10 · Common errorsInstalling unknown extensions (supply-chain risk); committing personal settings; conflicting formatters.
11 · Security considerationsInstall extensions only from verified publishers and the company list; enable Workspace Trust; keep secrets out of editor settings.
12 · DocumentationEditor setup steps in README.md ("Getting started").
13 · Practical assignmentConfigure a workspace with debug configs for frontend and backend.
14 · AssessmentPerform five editing tasks within a time limit using shortcuts only.
15 · Approval gateMentor sign-off.

Read: VS Code documentation

L5.4 · Code Reviews

EssentialFree4 h
1 · DefinitionA code review is a structured check of a change by another engineer before it merges - for correctness, security, readability, tests and standards.
2 · Business purposeReviews catch defects when they are cheapest to fix, spread knowledge and protect the client from one person's mistake. Every production change needs a second person's review.
3 · Real-world exampleThe reviewer notices an unvalidated query parameter in a new endpoint and requests a fix before merge - avoiding a possible SQL injection.
4 · PrerequisitesL5.1, L5.2.
5 · Tools & installationGitHub pull-request review, checklists, linters, CI results.

6 · Step-by-step procedure

  1. Author - keep the PR small (under about 400 changed lines), explain what and why, attach screenshots or test evidence.
  2. Reviewer - read the description, run the checks, review tests first, then code; comment on the code, not the person.
  3. Classify comments - blocker, suggestion, question, nit.
  4. Author responds to every comment; reviewer approves only when blockers are resolved.
  5. Merge with squash and a conventional commit message.

7 · Complete example

## What and why
Adds server-side date validation to booking creation (Closes #42).

## How tested
- [x] Unit tests added (12 cases)
- [x] Manual test in staging (screenshot attached)

## Checklist
- [x] No secrets - [x] Migrations reviewed - [x] Docs updated - [x] Accessibility checked

8 · Expected output

A completed PR template and a review thread with labelled comments and an approval.
9 · VerificationReview checklist (Section 9.4) completed; CI green; no unresolved threads.
10 · Common errorsRubber-stamp approvals; reviewing 2,000-line PRs; style debates that linters should settle; author merging own PR on production repositories.
11 · Security considerationsReviewer checks authentication, authorisation, validation, secrets, logging of personal data and dependency changes.
12 · DocumentationReview checklist in CONTRIBUTING.md.
13 · Practical assignmentReview three PRs from the sample repository and write constructive comments.
14 · AssessmentMentor rates review quality - found at least 5 of 7 planted issues.
15 · Approval gateMentor sign-off; reviewer rights granted after the gate.

L5.5 · Testing

EssentialFree14 h
1 · DefinitionTesting proves the software behaves as required. Layers - unit tests (one function), integration tests (several parts, e.g. API + database), end-to-end (E2E) tests (a real browser, e.g. Playwright), plus API tests (Postman/Newman) and manual exploratory testing.
2 · Business purposeAutomated tests let us change code fast without breaking the client's business, and provide evidence at acceptance.
3 · Real-world exampleA Playwright test opens the site on a phone-sized viewport, books a slot and asserts the confirmation text. It runs on every pull request.
4 · PrerequisitesL2.3, L3.1.
5 · Tools & installationVitest/Jest, Pytest, Playwright (free), Postman + Newman (free tier), coverage tools (coverage.py, c8).

6 · Step-by-step procedure

  1. Write unit tests for business rules first (test pyramid - many unit, fewer integration, few E2E).
  2. Write an API integration test with a throw-away database.
  3. Install Playwright and write one critical-path E2E test.
  4. Run all tests in CI; fail the build on failure.
  5. Track coverage as a guide, not a goal (aim for the important rules at 100%).

7 · Complete example

// tests/booking.spec.ts  -  run with: npx playwright test
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('visitor can request a booking on mobile', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.setViewportSize({ width: 390, height: 844 });
  await page.goto('/');
  await page.getByRole('link', { name: 'Book now' }).click();
  await page.getByLabel('Name').fill('Asha');
  await page.getByLabel('Email').fill('asha@example.com');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Confirm booking' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole('status')).toContainText('Booking confirmed');
});

8 · Expected output

Running 1 test using 1 worker
  1 passed (3.2s)
(an HTML report is written to playwright-report/)
9 · VerificationThe test fails when you break the feature on purpose, and passes when fixed (prove the test can fail).
10 · Common errorsFlaky tests using fixed sleeps; tests that depend on each other; testing implementation details; no test data cleanup; only testing the happy path.
11 · Security considerationsNever run tests against production data; use synthetic data; keep test credentials out of the repository.
12 · DocumentationTest plan and results in qa/ (see QA checklist, Appendix A6).
13 · Practical assignmentAdd unit, integration and two E2E tests to Project 3 with a CI run.
14 · AssessmentWrite tests for a given buggy function so that the bug is detected.
15 · Approval gateCI green with the required test layers.

Read: Playwright docs

L5.6 · Docker

EssentialFree10 h
1 · DefinitionDocker packages an application and everything it needs into an image that runs the same everywhere as a container. Docker Compose runs several containers together (app, database, cache).
2 · Business purposeContainers remove "works on my machine", make onboarding a one-command task and give repeatable deployments. Docker Desktop licensing for larger companies is paid - check Docker's current terms; alternatives include Podman and Colima.
3 · Real-world exampledocker compose up starts the API, the PostgreSQL database and Mailpit identical to what staging runs.
4 · PrerequisitesL5.1, L3.1, L4.1.
5 · Tools & installationDocker Engine / Docker Desktop, Docker Compose v2, a registry (GitHub Container Registry, Docker Hub, ECR).

6 · Step-by-step procedure

  1. Write a Dockerfile - small base image, non-root user, dependencies cached before code.
  2. Add .dockerignore (exclude .git, node_modules, .env).
  3. Write compose.yaml with the app, postgres and a named volume.
  4. Build, run and read logs; use health checks.
  5. Scan the image for vulnerabilities (Trivy, Docker Scout).

7 · Complete example

# Dockerfile (FastAPI)
FROM python:3.12-slim
ENV PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY src/ ./src/
RUN useradd -m appuser
USER appuser
EXPOSE 8000
HEALTHCHECK CMD python -c "import urllib.request as u; u.urlopen('http://localhost:8000/health')"
CMD ["uvicorn", "src.main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]

8 · Expected output

$ docker compose up -d
[+] Running 3/3  api  db  mailpit
$ curl localhost:8000/health
{"status":"ok"}
9 · Verificationdocker compose ps shows all services healthy; destroying and recreating containers keeps database data (volume).
10 · Common errorsRunning as root; secrets baked into images; using latest tags; huge images; storing data inside the container filesystem.
11 · Security considerationsPin versions, use minimal bases, non-root user, scan images, never mount the Docker socket, keep .env out of the image.
12 · Documentationdeployment/docker/README.md - build, run, environment variables, ports.
13 · Practical assignmentContainerise Project 4 (app + DB) and make it start with one command.
14 · AssessmentExplain image vs container vs volume and fix three Dockerfile problems.
15 · Approval gateTech Lead reviews Dockerfile and compose files.

Read: Docker docs

L5.7 · CI/CD with GitHub Actions

EssentialFree10 h
1 · DefinitionContinuous Integration (CI) automatically builds and tests every change. Continuous Delivery/Deployment (CD) automatically releases a tested build to staging, then production after approval. GitHub Actions runs workflows defined in .github/workflows/*.yml. Included free minutes differ by plan - check GitHub's current limits.
2 · Business purposeAutomation makes releases frequent, boring and safe; it enforces the quality gates for every client project.
3 · Real-world exampleMerging to main builds the Docker image, runs tests and deploys to staging. A manual approval promotes the same image to production.
4 · PrerequisitesL5.2, L5.5, L5.6.
5 · Tools & installationGitHub Actions, environments with required reviewers, GitHub Secrets, OIDC to cloud providers (no long-lived keys), a container registry.

6 · Step-by-step procedure

  1. Create a CI workflow - install, lint, type-check, test, build.
  2. Cache dependencies; run on pull_request and push to main.
  3. Add a security job (dependency audit, secret scan, image scan).
  4. Add a deploy job to staging, then a production job gated by environment approval.
  5. Pin actions to a version and use least-privilege permissions.

7 · Complete example

# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: CI
on:
  pull_request:
  push: { branches: [main] }
permissions: { contents: read }
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: 22, cache: npm }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run lint
      - run: npx tsc --noEmit
      - run: npm test -- --run
      - run: npm run build

8 · Expected output

A green check on the pull request; failures show the failing step log.
9 · VerificationBreak a test on purpose - the PR is blocked; fix it - the PR turns green.
10 · Common errorsSecrets echoed in logs; unpinned third-party actions; deploying from forks; no rollback step; tests that pass locally but fail in CI due to hidden state.
11 · Security considerationsLeast-privilege permissions, OIDC instead of stored cloud keys, environment protection for production, review changes to workflow files like production code.
12 · DocumentationPipeline description and rollback procedure in docs/deployment.md.
13 · Practical assignmentBuild a CI + staging CD pipeline for Project 4.
14 · AssessmentExplain each pipeline stage and show how a rollback is performed.
15 · Approval gateTech Lead approves pipeline and rollback test.

Read: GitHub Actions docs

L5.8 · Cloud Deployment

EssentialPaid14 h
1 · DefinitionCloud deployment runs the application on infrastructure rented from AWS, Azure or Google Cloud (or platforms such as Vercel, Netlify, Cloudflare). Typical building blocks - compute (VM, container service, serverless), managed database, object storage, load balancer, DNS, CDN, secrets manager.
2 · Business purposeProduction needs repeatable, secure, monitored infrastructure with cost controls. The right level of cloud for the project avoids both fragile single servers and expensive over-engineering.
3 · Real-world exampleA small business app runs as one container service + managed PostgreSQL + CDN; an enterprise SaaS uses a load-balanced container cluster, managed database with replicas and WAF.
4 · PrerequisitesL5.6, L5.7, L1.5.
5 · Tools & installationAWS (App Runner, ECS, EC2, RDS, S3, CloudFront), Azure (App Service, Container Apps, Azure DB), GCP (Cloud Run, Cloud SQL), Cloudflare (DNS, CDN, WAF, Pages), Terraform (infrastructure as code). Always price with the provider's official calculator.

6 · Step-by-step procedure

  1. Choose the provider and service model per the stack decision tree; record an ADR.
  2. Create separate dev, staging and production environments (separate accounts/projects where possible).
  3. Provision with infrastructure as code or a documented checklist; set budgets and cost alerts first.
  4. Deploy through CI/CD; store secrets in the provider's secret manager.
  5. Put the site behind HTTPS and a CDN/WAF; restrict database access to the private network.

7 · Complete example

# Example: deploy a container to Google Cloud Run (illustrative - verify flags in current docs)
gcloud run deploy clinic-api \
  --image ghcr.io/vel-org/clinic-api:1.4.0 \
  --region asia-south1 \
  --set-secrets DATABASE_URL=clinic-db-url:latest \
  --allow-unauthenticated \
  --min-instances 0 --max-instances 3

8 · Expected output

Service URL printed; revision `clinic-api-00007` receives 100% of traffic; rollback = route traffic to the previous revision.
9 · VerificationSmoke test passes (/health), HTTPS valid, logs visible, billing alert exists, rollback tested.
10 · Common errorsPublic database; admin keys in the repository; one shared account for everything; no budget alert; manual console changes nobody records.
11 · Security considerationsLeast-privilege IAM, MFA on root/admin, private networking, encryption at rest and in transit, WAF, regular patching, audit logging.
12 · DocumentationArchitecture diagram, environment table, access list and cost estimate in docs/deployment.md.
13 · Practical assignmentDeploy Project 4 to a free/low-cost tier in one provider with HTTPS and a custom domain.
14 · AssessmentWhiteboard the production design for a medium client and justify cost vs reliability.
15 · Approval gateDeployment checklist (Appendix A7) fully completed.

Read: AWS Documentation · Azure Documentation · Google Cloud Documentation · Cloudflare Docs

L5.9 · Logging

EssentialFree4 h
1 · DefinitionLogging records events the application produces - requests, errors, business events. Structured logs (JSON with fixed fields) can be searched and aggregated; log levels (DEBUG, INFO, WARNING, ERROR) separate noise from signal.
2 · Business purposeLogs are the first tool for diagnosing production problems and for audit trails, but they can also leak personal data if careless.
3 · Real-world exampleA customer says "my payment failed". Searching the request id in the logs shows the gateway returned card_declined at 14:03.
4 · PrerequisitesL3.7.
5 · Tools & installationPython logging/structlog, Node pino, Docker logs, cloud log services (CloudWatch, Azure Monitor, Cloud Logging), Loki/Grafana, ELK; Sentry for exceptions.

6 · Step-by-step procedure

  1. Choose log levels and a JSON format with timestamp, level, message, request id, user id (not email).
  2. Log at boundaries - request in/out, external calls, errors, important business events.
  3. Never log passwords, tokens, full card numbers or national IDs.
  4. Send logs to a central place with a retention period.
  5. Create two saved searches - "all errors in 24 h" and "trace one request".

7 · Complete example

import json, logging, sys

class JsonFormatter(logging.Formatter):
    def format(self, r: logging.LogRecord) -> str:
        return json.dumps({"ts": self.formatTime(r), "level": r.levelname, "msg": r.getMessage(),
                           "logger": r.name, **getattr(r, "ctx", {})})

h = logging.StreamHandler(sys.stdout); h.setFormatter(JsonFormatter())
log = logging.getLogger("api"); log.addHandler(h); log.setLevel(logging.INFO)
log.info("booking created", extra={"ctx": {"rid": "3f9a2c1b", "booking_id": 981, "user_id": 42}})

8 · Expected output

{"ts": "2026-11-04 10:32:11,408", "level": "INFO", "msg": "booking created", "logger": "api", "rid": "3f9a2c1b", "booking_id": 981, "user_id": 42}
9 · VerificationA request id from the response header finds every related log line within seconds.
10 · Common errorsprint debugging in production; logging whole request bodies; no retention policy; logs only on the server's disk; alert fatigue from noisy logs.
11 · Security considerationsMask personal data; restrict log access; define retention (privacy law); treat logs as sensitive.
12 · DocumentationLog format, fields, levels and retention table in docs/security.md.
13 · Practical assignmentAdd structured logging and one saved search to Project 4.
14 · AssessmentDiagnose a seeded incident from a log file within 15 minutes.
15 · Approval gateMentor sign-off.

L5.10 · Monitoring and Alerting

EssentialFree6 h
1 · DefinitionMonitoring measures the health of a system continuously. The key signals are latency, traffic, errors and saturation. Uptime checks test the site from outside; alerts notify a person when a threshold is crossed; an SLO is a target such as 99.9% availability.
2 · Business purposeWe should know about a failure before the client does. Monitoring is also what makes a maintenance contract credible and billable.
3 · Real-world exampleAn uptime check on /health every minute emails and messages the on-call engineer after two failures; a dashboard shows p95 latency and error rate.
4 · PrerequisitesL5.8, L5.9.
5 · Tools & installationUptimeRobot/Better Stack/Checkly (free tiers - check limits), Grafana + Prometheus, cloud monitors, Sentry, Lighthouse CI.

6 · Step-by-step procedure

  1. Add a /health endpoint that checks the database and critical dependencies.
  2. Configure an external uptime check with SSL-expiry alert.
  3. Create a dashboard - requests, p95 latency, 5xx rate, CPU/memory, disk, DB connections.
  4. Define alerts that need action (not noise) and an escalation path.
  5. Test one alert end to end.

7 · Complete example

@app.get("/health")
def health(db=Depends(get_db)):
    try:
        db.execute("SELECT 1")
    except Exception:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=503, detail="database unavailable")
    return {"status": "ok", "version": APP_VERSION}

8 · Expected output

`200 {"status":"ok","version":"1.4.0"}` normally; `503` when the database is down, which triggers the alert.
9 · VerificationStop the database in staging - an alert reaches the on-call channel within 5 minutes.
10 · Common errorsAlerts nobody owns; monitoring only CPU; health checks that always return 200; no certificate-expiry or backup-failure alerts.
11 · Security considerationsKeep /health free of sensitive details; restrict dashboards; monitor failed-login spikes and unusual traffic.
12 · DocumentationMonitoring plan - checks, thresholds, owners, escalation - in docs/deployment.md.
13 · Practical assignmentBuild monitoring and alerts for the Project 4 deployment.
14 · AssessmentExplain the difference between an alert, a dashboard and a log, and when each is used.
15 · Approval gateAlert fire-drill passed.

Read: web.dev - Measure performance

L5.11 · Web Application Security

EssentialFree16 h
1 · DefinitionWeb application security protects confidentiality, integrity and availability. The reference is the OWASP Top 10 (broken access control, cryptographic failures, injection, insecure design, misconfiguration, vulnerable components, authentication failures, integrity failures, logging failures, SSRF) and the OWASP ASVS checklist.
2 · Business purposeA breach harms the client's customers and reputation and ends our relationship. Security is designed in, reviewed at every stage and verified before release - but we never claim a system is \"secure\" or \"hack-proof\".
3 · Real-world exampleA pre-release review finds a customer-id parameter that returns other customers' invoices (IDOR); fixed with an ownership check and a regression test.
4 · PrerequisitesL3.3 to L3.8, L5.7.
5 · Tools & installationOWASP ZAP (free), npm audit / pip-audit, Dependabot, Semgrep, Gitleaks, Trivy, Mozilla Observatory / securityheaders.com, browser DevTools.

6 · Step-by-step procedure

  1. Threat-model the feature - assets, entry points, abuse cases.
  2. Apply controls - validation, parameterised queries, output encoding, auth and access checks, CSRF protection, rate limiting.
  3. Set security headers (CSP, HSTS, X-Content-Type-Options, frame protections, Referrer-Policy).
  4. Scan - dependencies, secrets, containers and the running app (ZAP baseline).
  5. Triage findings by severity; fix criticals before release; document accepted risks with the client.

7 · Complete example

# Nginx security headers (tune the CSP for each project)
add_header Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains" always;
add_header X-Content-Type-Options "nosniff" always;
add_header Referrer-Policy "strict-origin-when-cross-origin" always;
add_header X-Frame-Options "DENY" always;
add_header Content-Security-Policy "default-src 'self'; img-src 'self' data:; frame-ancestors 'none'" always;

8 · Expected output

securityheaders.com shows A or better; ZAP baseline reports no high-severity findings.
9 · VerificationA written security report lists scans run, findings, fixes and accepted risks, and is attached to the release.
10 · Common errorsRelying on the frontend for protection; disabling TLS verification "to make it work"; default admin passwords; verbose error pages; unpatched dependencies.
11 · Security considerationsThis module is the control framework itself - apply the OWASP ASVS level agreed in the SOW; use the least privilege everywhere; plan for incident response and responsible disclosure.
12 · Documentationdocs/security.md - threat model, controls, scan results, incident contacts.
13 · Practical assignmentRun a full security review (manual + ZAP + dependency scan) on Project 4 and fix all high findings.
14 · AssessmentAttack-and-defend lab - exploit three seeded vulnerabilities, then patch them.
15 · Approval gateLevel 5 completion review - all modules signed; Security review signed by Tech Lead.

Read: OWASP · OWASP Top 10 · OWASP Cheat Sheet Series

Level assessment summary

Level Written Practical Oral (Technical Lead)
1 20-question quiz, pass 80% Whiteboard request path; DNS plan 10 minutes
2 30-question quiz Timed UI task; component review 15 minutes
3 Security quiz Attack-test of your API (five attacks) 20 minutes
4 SQL test (10 queries / 60 min) Restore drill within RTO 15 minutes
5 OWASP and DevOps quiz Pipeline + rollback demonstration; security review 30 minutes
Part A · Foundations

4. Technology Stack and Tool Selection

The department teaches and uses a broad toolbox, but selects technology according to project requirements instead of forcing one stack on every client. This section classifies each tool as essential or optional, and free or paid. Licence terms, free-tier limits and prices change - always check the official page on the day of use.

Tool classification

Tool / technology Role Essential or optional Free or paid Notes
HTML, CSS, JavaScript Core web languages Essential Free (open standards) MDN and the HTML Living Standard are the references
TypeScript Typed JavaScript Essential (all new projects) Free (open source) strict mode on
React UI library Essential Free (open source) Default for interactive UIs
Next.js React framework (SSR/SSG, routing, API) Essential Free (open source); hosting may cost Alternatives - Astro, Remix, Vite SPA, Nuxt, SvelteKit
Node.js JavaScript runtime / backend Essential Free (open source) LTS versions only for production
FastAPI Python API framework Essential (API-first products) Free (open source) Pydantic validation, OpenAPI docs
Django Python full-stack framework Optional (admin/ORM-heavy projects) Free (open source) Strong built-in admin and auth
PostgreSQL Relational database Essential (default) Free (open source); managed hosting is paid
MySQL / MariaDB Relational database Optional (WordPress/WooCommerce, legacy) Free (community edition); managed hosting is paid
Git Version control Essential Free
GitHub Hosting, PRs, Actions Essential Free and paid plans - verify current limits Organisation account with MFA
VS Code Editor Essential Free Shared extension pack
Docker Containers Essential Engine free; Docker Desktop licence terms vary by company size - verify Podman is an alternative
Playwright End-to-end testing Essential (critical journeys) Free (open source) Runs in CI
Postman API testing Essential (or curl/Bruno/Insomnia) Free tier + paid plans - verify Export collections to Git
AWS / Azure / GCP Cloud hosting One essential per project Pay-as-you-go; free tiers have limits - verify Choose per client, region, budget
Cloudflare (or similar CDN) DNS, CDN, WAF, caching Optional but recommended Free and paid plans - verify Speed and DDoS protection
Terraform / OpenTofu Infrastructure as code Optional (medium/enterprise) Free (open source)
Sentry or similar Error tracking Recommended Free tier + paid - verify
Figma UI/UX design Essential for design work Free tier + paid - verify
Lighthouse, axe, ZAP Quality and security scans Essential Free

How to choose a stack

Criterion Questions to ask Effect on the choice
Content or application? Does the client mainly publish content, or do users log in and transact? Content - static/CMS; application - Next.js + API + database
Who edits content? Non-technical staff or developers? Staff - headless CMS or WordPress; developers - Markdown/Git
Traffic and growth Visitors per month now and in 12 months; peaks Low - managed platform; high - CDN, caching, scaling
Data sensitivity Personal, financial, health data? Higher - private networking, encryption, audit, stricter hosting region
Integrations Payment, ERP, CRM, SMS, WhatsApp Prefer providers with good SDKs and webhooks
Team skills Who maintains it after launch? Prefer stacks the client's team or ours can maintain
Budget and running cost Monthly cost the client can sustain Managed services trade money for time
Time to market Deadline Buy (Shopify, WordPress, SaaS) before build
Compliance and region Data residency, accessibility law, tax Choose provider regions accordingly

Standard stacks (starting points, not rules)

Project type Frontend Backend Database Hosting pattern
Brochure / landing page Astro or Next.js static Serverless function for forms - CDN static hosting
Corporate site with CMS Next.js Headless CMS (or WordPress) CMS-managed Managed platform + CDN
E-commerce (standard) Shopify / WooCommerce theme Platform Platform SaaS or managed WordPress
E-commerce (custom) Next.js FastAPI or Node PostgreSQL Container service + managed DB + CDN
Customer portal / admin Next.js + React FastAPI/Django/Node PostgreSQL Container service + managed DB
SaaS Next.js FastAPI/Node + queue worker PostgreSQL + cache Containers, CI/CD, monitoring, backups
Booking system Next.js FastAPI/Node PostgreSQL Container service + e-mail/SMS provider

Record the decision

Write an Architecture Decision Record (ADR) for every major choice (see L1.5 for the template): the context, at least two options, the decision, the consequences and the date any vendor facts were verified.

Licence and supply-chain rules

  • Use only software whose licence allows commercial use; record each dependency's licence (npm ls, pip-licenses).
  • Commit lock files (package-lock.json, poetry.lock/requirements.txt with hashes) and enable Dependabot.
  • Do not install unknown packages or extensions; check download counts, maintainers and recent activity.
  • Never paste client code or data into unapproved online tools or AI assistants. Use only company-approved tools and follow the client contract.
Part B · Client Delivery

5. Client Project Lifecycle: Stages 01-27

Every client project - whether a one-page site or a SaaS platform - follows these 27 stages in order. Small projects run stages quickly and combine documents; they never skip a gate. For each stage this section defines the purpose, responsible employee, inputs, procedure, outputs, tools, risks, verification, documentation and approval authority.

Phases and gates

Phase Stages Main output Key gate
1 - Win and define 1-6 Signed SOW, frozen scope Gate 05: SOW approved - work may start
2 - Design 7-10 Sitemap, approved UI/UX, architecture, database design Gate 08: design approved; Gate 10: DB design review
3 - Build 11-18 Working, integrated product in staging Code review on every pull request
4 - Verify and release 19-25 Tested, secured, deployed, live with HTTPS Gate 22: UAT sign-off before production
5 - Operate 26-27 Handover, maintenance, support Gate 26: signed handover certificate

Role abbreviations used in the stage tables

Abbreviation Role
PM Project Manager
TL Technical Lead
BD Business Development executive
UX UI/UX Designer
FE / BE / FS Frontend / Backend / Full-stack developer
QA QA engineer
DO DevOps engineer

Approval authority matrix

Decision Approves Informed
Accept the lead PM BD, TL
Scope and SOW Authorised commercial representative + client signatory PM, TL
Design Client sponsor UX, TL, FE
Architecture and database design TL PM, DO, client IT
Merge to main A reviewer who is not the author (TL for sensitive modules) Team
Release to staging TL PM, QA
UAT acceptance Client sponsor PM, QA
Production deployment (go/no-go) TL PM, client
Handover Client sponsor PM, TL, DO
Change request PM (impact) + client sponsor (cost/time) TL

DO NOT START IMPLEMENTATION

without (1) an approved scope and SOW, (2) agreed commercial terms and (3) written access authorisation. Access is granted to named individuals with individual accounts - never shared admin credentials.

Change-request procedure (applies from Stage 6 onwards)

  1. The client or a team member raises the change in writing (ticket or e-mail).
  2. The PM and TL assess impact on cost, time, risk and other features.
  3. The client approves the revised quote and timeline.
  4. An SOW addendum is signed before work begins; the change log is updated.

Stage definitions

Stage 01 — Lead Qualification

PurposeDecide quickly and honestly whether an enquiry is a good fit - budget, scope, timeline, decision-maker, risk - before spending delivery effort.
Responsible employeeBusiness Development executive (with Project Manager for technical fit).
InputsEnquiry (email, call, form, referral); company profile; rough idea and budget range.
Procedure
  1. Log the lead in the CRM with source, contact, need and date.
  2. Call within one working day; confirm who decides and who pays.
  3. Score the lead (budget, urgency, clarity, authority, fit) 1-5 each; pass at 15 or more.
  4. Screen for red flags - no budget, "copy this site exactly", unclear ownership of content, legal or ethical concerns.
  5. Book a discovery call or politely decline with a referral.
OutputsLead record with score; go/no-go decision; discovery meeting invite.
ToolsCRM or spreadsheet, calendar, email templates.
RisksChasing unqualified leads; promising price or dates before understanding scope; copyright-infringing requests.
VerificationSecond person reviews any lead scoring below 15 that is being pursued.
DocumentationLead qualification sheet (Appendix A3, part 1).
Approval authorityProject Manager approves go/no-go.

Gate 01

Qualified lead recorded and discovery call scheduled.

Stage 02 — Client Discovery

PurposeUnderstand the client's business, users, goals and constraints before proposing any solution.
Responsible employeeProject Manager (lead) with Technical Lead and UI/UX Designer attending.
InputsQualified lead; existing website/system access (read-only); brand materials.
Procedure
  1. Send the discovery questionnaire (Appendix A3) 2 days before the meeting.
  2. Run a 60-90 minute structured session - business goals, target users, current process, pain points, success measures.
  3. Ask about content (who writes it), branding, integrations, compliance and data sensitivity.
  4. Record decisions, assumptions and open questions; never assume.
  5. Send meeting minutes within 24 hours for the client to confirm.
OutputsCompleted questionnaire; confirmed meeting minutes; list of assumptions and open questions.
ToolsDiscovery questionnaire, video call, shared notes, Miro/FigJam.
RisksHidden stakeholders; vague goals; "we will know it when we see it"; undisclosed legacy systems.
VerificationClient replies "confirmed" to the minutes; open questions have owners and dates.
DocumentationDiscovery notes in docs/requirements.md (section "Discovery").
Approval authorityProject Manager; client sponsor confirms the minutes.

Gate 02

Client confirms the problem statement and goals in writing.

Stage 03 — Business and Technical Requirement Collection

PurposeTurn needs into clear, testable requirements - functional, non-functional, content, integration and compliance.
Responsible employeeBusiness analyst or Project Manager; Technical Lead for non-functional requirements.
InputsDiscovery minutes; existing assets; user stories; stakeholder list.
Procedure
  1. Write user stories - "As a [role] I want [goal] so that [benefit]" - each with acceptance criteria.
  2. Capture non-functional requirements - performance targets, availability, browsers/devices, accessibility level (WCAG 2.2 AA), SEO, languages, data retention, privacy.
  3. List integrations (payment, email, SMS, CRM, analytics) and who owns each account.
  4. Prioritise with MoSCoW (must, should, could, won't this time).
  5. Review line by line with the client; mark each requirement as agreed.
OutputsRequirements document with unique ids (REQ-001...), priorities and acceptance criteria.
ToolsRequirements template (Appendix A4), Jira/Linear/GitHub Projects, spreadsheet.
RisksAmbiguous words ("fast", "user-friendly"); gold-plating; missing compliance rules; unspoken dependencies.
VerificationEvery requirement is testable; each "must" has at least one acceptance test; Technical Lead confirms feasibility.
Documentationdocs/requirements.md (versioned in Git).
Approval authorityTechnical Lead (feasibility) and Project Manager; client signs off.

Stage 04 — Competitor and Market Research

PurposeLearn what good looks like in the client's market so design and features are informed, not guessed.
Responsible employeeProject Manager with UI/UX Designer.
InputsClient's competitors, target market, keywords, positioning.
Procedure
  1. Identify 3-5 direct competitors and 2 best-in-class references.
  2. Compare features, user journeys, pricing presentation, trust signals, speed and accessibility (Lighthouse, manual).
  3. Check search visibility with free tools (Google Search Console later, keyword planners).
  4. Note what to copy (patterns), what to avoid, and where the client can differentiate.
  5. Never copy text, images or code from competitors (copyright).
OutputsCompetitor matrix, opportunity list, recommended differentiators.
ToolsBrowser DevTools, Lighthouse, spreadsheet, public SEO tools.
RisksCopying; analysis paralysis; confusing taste with evidence.
VerificationFindings cite specific pages/screenshots with date; claims are checkable.
DocumentationResearch summary in docs/requirements.md (section "Market").
Approval authorityProject Manager.

Stage 05 — Scope and Statement of Work (SOW) Approval

PurposeCreate a binding agreement on what will be built, what will not, for how much and by when.
Responsible employeeProject Manager (author); Technical Lead (technical review); authorised commercial representative (price).
InputsApproved requirements; estimate (Section 8); risk list; legal templates.
Procedure
  1. Use the SOW template (Appendix A5) - objectives, in-scope, out-of-scope, deliverables, assumptions, client responsibilities, timeline, milestones, acceptance criteria, price and payment terms, warranty/support, change control, IP and confidentiality.
  2. Cost it with the costing workbook; include contingency; add a managed-service quote.
  3. Technical Lead reviews feasibility and estimate; PM reviews commercial terms.
  4. Send to client; address comments; obtain a signature (e-sign acceptable).
OutputsSigned SOW; approved estimate; project baseline.
ToolsSOW template, costing workbook, e-signature tool, legal review where needed.
RisksUndefined acceptance; scope creep; unlimited revisions; missing client responsibilities (content, access, approvals).
VerificationChecklist - every requirement mapped to an item; out-of-scope list present; payment milestones tied to deliverables.
DocumentationSigned SOW archived in the project folder; version recorded.
Approval authorityAuthorised commercial representative and client signatory.

Gate 05

No work starts without an approved SOW, agreed commercial terms and written access authorisation.

Stage 06 — Input/Output and Feature Freeze

PurposeLock the inputs the client must supply and the outputs we will deliver, and freeze the feature list so estimates stay valid.
Responsible employeeProject Manager; Technical Lead.
InputsSigned SOW; requirement list.
Procedure
  1. List client inputs - logo, brand colours, text, images, product data, third-party account access - with owners and due dates.
  2. List outputs - screens, endpoints, reports, emails, documentation, training.
  3. Agree the feature freeze date; after it, changes follow the change-request procedure only.
  4. Record the baseline in the project tracker (all items, estimates, acceptance criteria).
OutputsInput/output register; frozen feature list; change-control log opened.
ToolsProject board, register spreadsheet, change-request form.
RisksLate content (the top cause of delay); "small additions"; hidden dependencies on third parties.
VerificationClient confirms the register; each item has an owner and date.
DocumentationInput/output register in docs/requirements.md; change log in CHANGELOG.md and tracker.
Approval authorityProject Manager and client sponsor.

Gate 06

Client signs the feature freeze.

Stage 07 — Sitemap and Information Architecture

PurposeOrganise content and navigation so users find things easily and search engines understand the site.
Responsible employeeUI/UX Designer with Project Manager.
InputsRequirements; content inventory; keyword research; competitor findings.
Procedure
  1. Build a content inventory - every page, its owner and purpose.
  2. Draw the sitemap (hierarchy) and key user flows (e.g. visitor -> enquiry; customer -> checkout).
  3. Define navigation, URL structure (short, lowercase, readable) and page templates.
  4. Plan SEO basics - one primary topic per page, titles, meta descriptions, redirects for old URLs.
  5. Review with the client using a clickable outline.
OutputsSitemap diagram, user-flow diagrams, URL map, redirect list.
ToolsFigJam/Miro/Whimsical, spreadsheet, Screaming Frog (free tier) for existing sites.
RisksToo many top-level menu items; orphan pages; breaking old URLs and losing rankings.
VerificationCard-sort or 5-user quick test on the outline; every page reachable in 3 clicks.
DocumentationSitemap and URL map in docs/requirements.md.
Approval authorityProject Manager; client approves sitemap.

Stage 08 — UI/UX Design Approval

PurposeAgree what the product looks like and how it behaves before any code is written.
Responsible employeeUI/UX Designer (author); client sponsor (approver).
InputsSitemap; brand assets; competitor matrix; accessibility requirements.
Procedure
  1. Create low-fidelity wireframes for key pages and flows; review with the client.
  2. Build a design system - colours, typography, spacing, components, states.
  3. Produce high-fidelity mock-ups for desktop and mobile (mobile-first).
  4. Check contrast, tap-target size and focus order against WCAG 2.2 AA.
  5. Build a clickable prototype; run a quick usability test; record client approval of final screens.
OutputsWireframes; design tokens; high-fidelity screens; prototype; developer hand-off notes.
ToolsFigma, accessibility checkers, Stark/contrast tools, Maze or manual user tests.
RisksEndless revisions; designs that ignore real content; inaccessible colour choices; no mobile design.
VerificationDesign review checklist; client approves in writing; Frontend Lead confirms feasibility.
DocumentationFigma link, version, approval email stored with the project.
Approval authorityClient sponsor (design); Technical Lead (feasibility).

Gate 08

Written design approval - changes after this follow change control.

Stage 09 — Technical Architecture

PurposeChoose and document the stack, structure and infrastructure that will meet the requirements at the agreed cost and risk.
Responsible employeeTechnical Lead (author); DevOps engineer; client's IT contact (review).
InputsRequirements; non-functional targets; budget; team skills; compliance needs.
Procedure
  1. Compare at least two options (e.g. CMS vs custom, monolith vs services, managed vs self-hosted) against cost, security, scalability, maintainability.
  2. Draw system, data-flow, deployment and security-boundary diagrams.
  3. Define environments (dev, staging, production), hosting, CDN, email, storage, monitoring.
  4. Record each major choice as an Architecture Decision Record (ADR).
  5. Estimate hosting and third-party running costs from official pricing pages.
OutputsArchitecture document; ADRs; environment plan; running-cost estimate.
Toolsdraw.io/Excalidraw, ADR template, vendor pricing calculators.
RisksOver-engineering; resume-driven technology; hidden vendor lock-in; running costs not shared with the client.
VerificationPeer review by another senior engineer; cost figures traceable to vendor pages with date.
Documentationdocs/architecture.md and docs/adr/.
Approval authorityTechnical Lead; client IT contact where applicable.

Stage 10 — Database Design

PurposeModel the client's data correctly, securely and efficiently before building features on top of it.
Responsible employeeBackend developer or full-stack developer (author); Technical Lead (reviewer).
InputsRequirements; architecture; data-protection requirements.
Procedure
  1. Identify entities, attributes and relationships; normalise to 3NF.
  2. Define keys, constraints, indexes for expected queries and audit columns.
  3. Classify personal and sensitive data; define retention and encryption needs.
  4. Write the ER diagram and data dictionary; review with Technical Lead.
  5. Plan migrations and seed data; plan backup (RPO/RTO).
OutputsER diagram; data dictionary; initial migration plan; backup plan.
Toolsdbdiagram.io/pgModeler, SQL DDL, migration tool.
RisksPoor modelling that is expensive to change; money in floats; no constraints; collecting unnecessary personal data.
VerificationWalk through 10 real scenarios on the model; Technical Lead signs the review checklist.
Documentationdocs/database-design.md.
Approval authorityTechnical Lead.

Gate 10

Database design review passed before implementation.

Stage 11 — Development Environment Setup

PurposeGive every engineer an identical, secure, reproducible working environment.
Responsible employeeDevOps engineer or Technical Lead; each developer completes onboarding checks.
InputsArchitecture; stack decisions; access list.
Procedure
  1. Provision company-approved laptop with disk encryption and screen lock.
  2. Install the toolchain from the README (Node/Python versions pinned, Docker, VS Code extension pack).
  3. Create .env from .env.example using development-only values.
  4. Run docker compose up and the test suite - both must pass on a fresh clone.
  5. Give each person individual accounts (GitHub, cloud, tracker) with MFA.
OutputsWorking dev environment per developer; verified README setup steps.
ToolsGit, Docker, VS Code, password manager, MFA app.
RisksShared accounts; "works on my machine"; production credentials on laptops.
VerificationA new teammate follows the README and runs the app within 30 minutes.
DocumentationREADME.md getting-started section.
Approval authorityTechnical Lead.

Stage 12 — GitHub Repository Creation

PurposeCreate the single source of truth for code and documentation with protection and automation in place from day one.
Responsible employeeTechnical Lead or DevOps engineer.
InputsProject name; team list; standard repository template.
Procedure
  1. Create a private repository in the company organisation from the template (folder structure, .gitignore, .env.example, PR template, CI workflow).
  2. Protect main and develop - PR required, approvals, passing checks, no force push.
  3. Add CODEOWNERS; enable secret scanning and Dependabot.
  4. Create labels, milestones and the initial issues from the frozen requirements.
  5. Add team members with least privilege.
OutputsConfigured repository; first commit; issue backlog.
ToolsGitHub, gh CLI, template repository.
RisksPublic repository by mistake; committed secrets; unprotected branches.
VerificationRepository settings checklist; a test push to main is rejected.
DocumentationREADME.md, CONTRIBUTING.md.
Approval authorityTechnical Lead.

Stage 13 — Frontend Development

PurposeBuild the user interface exactly to the approved design, responsive, accessible and fast.
Responsible employeeFrontend developer (or full-stack developer); UI/UX Designer reviews.
InputsApproved design and tokens; API specification (or mock server); content.
Procedure
  1. Implement design tokens, layout and shared components first.
  2. Build pages from the design with mock data; then connect to the real API.
  3. Handle loading, empty, error and success states for every data view.
  4. Test at 360, 768, 1024 and 1440 px; keyboard-only; screen reader spot check.
  5. Optimise images, fonts and bundle size; add SEO metadata.
  6. Open small pull requests; demo each milestone in staging.
OutputsWorking UI in staging; component library; unit/component tests.
ToolsReact/Next.js, TypeScript, Tailwind or CSS modules, Storybook (optional), Playwright, Lighthouse.
RisksDesign drift; inaccessible components; performance regressions; hard-coded content.
VerificationDesign review against mock-ups; Lighthouse targets; accessibility checks; PR reviews.
DocumentationComponent notes in frontend/README.md; Storybook where used.
Approval authorityUI/UX Designer (visual match); Technical Lead (code).

Stage 14 — Backend Development

PurposeImplement the business rules, API and security controls that make the product work.
Responsible employeeBackend developer (or full-stack developer).
InputsApproved API specification; database design; business rules.
Procedure
  1. Implement endpoints in the order of the critical user journeys.
  2. Keep routes thin; put rules in a tested service layer.
  3. Validate all input; return the standard error format; log with request ids.
  4. Write unit and integration tests alongside each feature.
  5. Add rate limiting, CORS rules and security headers.
OutputsWorking API in staging; automated tests; OpenAPI document.
ToolsFastAPI/Django/Node framework, Pytest/Jest, Postman, linters.
RisksLogic duplicated in the frontend; missing authorisation checks; unbounded queries; secrets in code.
VerificationTest suite green in CI; peer code review; API contract tests against the spec.
Documentationdocs/api-specification.md (kept in sync with OpenAPI).
Approval authorityTechnical Lead.

Stage 15 — API Integration

PurposeConnect frontend, backend and the client's other systems through stable, documented, tested interfaces.
Responsible employeeFull-stack developer; Technical Lead.
InputsAPI specification; third-party API documentation and sandbox keys.
Procedure
  1. Generate or write a typed API client; centralise base URL, auth and error handling.
  2. Integrate screen by screen; remove mocks when the real endpoint passes tests.
  3. Add timeouts, retries (only for safe calls) and circuit-breaking for third parties.
  4. Test failure cases - 401, 403, 404, 422, 500, network down.
OutputsFully integrated flows; integration test results.
ToolsOpenAPI generators, fetch/axios, Postman/Newman, mock servers.
RisksContract drift; breaking changes; unhandled third-party downtime.
VerificationEnd-to-end test of each critical journey in staging.
DocumentationIntegration notes and error handling table in docs/api-specification.md.
Approval authorityTechnical Lead.

Stage 16 — Database Implementation

PurposeCreate and manage the real schema through versioned migrations with seed data and backups.
Responsible employeeBackend developer; DevOps engineer (backup/hosting).
InputsApproved database design; chosen database service.
Procedure
  1. Write migrations; run them on a fresh database in CI.
  2. Create least-privilege application and migration users.
  3. Load seed/reference data (no real personal data).
  4. Add indexes for measured queries; review plans with EXPLAIN.
  5. Enable automated backups and run a restore test.
OutputsSchema in dev and staging built only from migrations; backup/restore evidence.
ToolsAlembic/Django/Prisma migrations, psql, pgAdmin/DBeaver.
RisksManual schema edits; slow queries; missing backups; data loss during migration.
VerificationSchema diff between environments is empty; restore test passes within the RTO.
Documentationdocs/database-design.md updated; migration notes in database/migrations/.
Approval authorityTechnical Lead.

Stage 17 — Authentication and Permissions

PurposeEnsure only the right people can sign in and perform the right actions.
Responsible employeeBackend developer; Technical Lead reviews every change.
InputsAccess matrix (roles x actions); security requirements; identity provider decision.
Procedure
  1. Implement registration, login, logout, token/session handling and password reset (or integrate an identity provider).
  2. Implement the access matrix (RBAC + ownership checks) server-side.
  3. Add rate limiting, lockout/backoff, secure cookies and CSRF protection.
  4. Add MFA for admin users where the SOW requires it.
  5. Write tests for every cell of the access matrix and the five standard attacks.
OutputsAuthentication and authorisation implemented and tested; access matrix document.
ToolsArgon2/bcrypt, JWT or sessions, OAuth/OIDC provider, OWASP ZAP.
RisksBroken access control (OWASP #1); weak password storage; session fixation; open registration abuse.
VerificationSecurity review checklist; negative tests; peer review by the Technical Lead.
Documentationdocs/security.md (flows, token lifetimes, access matrix).
Approval authorityTechnical Lead.

Stage 18 — Payment and Third-Party Integrations

PurposeSafely connect payment gateways and other external services so money, messages and data flow correctly.
Responsible employeeBackend developer; Technical Lead; Project Manager for client account setup.
InputsClient-owned gateway/provider accounts; sandbox keys; business rules for refunds, taxes and failures.
Procedure
  1. Use the provider's hosted checkout or tokenisation so card data never touches our servers (reduces PCI scope).
  2. Create orders server-side; verify payment by a signed webhook, not by the browser redirect alone.
  3. Make webhook handling idempotent; store provider ids; handle failed, pending and refunded states.
  4. Test in the sandbox - success, decline, timeout, duplicate webhook, refund.
  5. Store provider API keys in the secret manager; rotate on staff changes.
OutputsWorking integrations; reconciliation report; sandbox test evidence.
ToolsGateway SDKs (for example Razorpay, Stripe, PayPal - confirm availability, fees and compliance for the client's country on each official site), Postman, ngrok-style tunnels for webhooks in dev.
RisksDouble charging; unverified webhooks; storing card data; wrong tax or rounding; gateway downtime.
VerificationTest matrix executed and signed; finance contact reconciles test transactions.
DocumentationIntegration runbook and flow diagram in docs/architecture.md.
Approval authorityTechnical Lead and client finance contact.

Stage 19 — Unit and Integration Testing

PurposeProve with repeatable automated tests that each part and the connected parts behave as required.
Responsible employeeQA engineer with developers.
InputsRequirements with acceptance criteria; test data; staging build.
Procedure
  1. Write a test plan mapping every requirement id to test cases.
  2. Developers maintain unit tests; QA adds integration, API (Postman/Newman) and E2E (Playwright) suites.
  3. Cover happy path, edge cases, invalid input and permission failures.
  4. Run cross-browser (Chrome, Edge, Firefox, Safari) and device checks.
  5. Log defects with steps, evidence and severity; retest after fixes.
OutputsTest plan, automated suites, defect log, test report.
ToolsPytest/Vitest, Playwright, Postman/Newman, BrowserStack or real devices.
RisksTest gaps; flaky tests; testing only on developer machines.
Verification100% of must-have requirements have a passing test; no open critical/high defects.
Documentationqa/test-plan.md, qa/test-report.md.
Approval authorityQA engineer (results); Technical Lead (release readiness).

Stage 20 — Security and Performance Testing

PurposeFind and fix vulnerabilities and slowness before the client's customers do.
Responsible employeeTechnical Lead or security-trained engineer; DevOps for load tests.
InputsStaging environment; threat model; performance targets.
Procedure
  1. Scan dependencies, secrets, containers and code (Dependabot/npm audit/pip-audit, Gitleaks, Trivy, Semgrep).
  2. Run OWASP ZAP baseline against staging; manually test top abuse cases (IDOR, XSS, injection, upload abuse).
  3. Check headers, TLS configuration, cookies and CORS.
  4. Run Lighthouse/WebPageTest; load-test critical endpoints (k6 or Locust) at the agreed traffic with p95 and error-rate targets.
  5. Fix findings by severity; retest; document accepted risks.
OutputsSecurity report, performance report, fixed-findings list.
ToolsOWASP ZAP, Gitleaks, Trivy, Semgrep, Lighthouse, k6/Locust.
RisksTesting production by mistake; ignoring "medium" findings forever; unrealistic load profiles.
VerificationNo open critical or high findings; performance targets met or exceptions agreed in writing.
Documentationdocs/security.md (results) and qa/ reports. Never claim the system is "secure" - state what was tested.
Approval authorityTechnical Lead; client acknowledges accepted risks.

Stage 21 — Staging Deployment

PurposeRun the release candidate in a production-like environment for final verification.
Responsible employeeDevOps engineer.
InputsRelease candidate tag; deployment runbook; staging environment.
Procedure
  1. Deploy the exact artefact (Docker image) that will go to production via the pipeline.
  2. Apply migrations; load realistic synthetic data (no real personal data).
  3. Configure staging domain with HTTPS and basic protection (password or IP allow-list); block indexing.
  4. Run smoke tests and the full E2E suite.
  5. Rehearse rollback once.
OutputsStaging URL; smoke-test results; rehearsed rollback.
ToolsGitHub Actions, Docker, cloud platform, Cloudflare.
RisksStaging differs from production; staging indexed by search engines; real data copied.
VerificationSame image digest later promoted to production; configuration differences listed and justified.
DocumentationRelease notes draft in CHANGELOG.md; deployment log.
Approval authorityTechnical Lead.

Stage 22 — Client Review and User Acceptance Testing (UAT)

PurposeLet the client verify the product against the agreed acceptance criteria.
Responsible employeeProject Manager (coordination); QA engineer (support).
InputsStaging URL; UAT script; acceptance criteria from the SOW.
Procedure
  1. Hold a demo walkthrough; share the UAT script and test accounts.
  2. Give a fixed review window (for example 5 working days) and one consolidated feedback round.
  3. Triage feedback - defect (fix), change request (quote), or preference (discuss).
  4. Fix defects, redeploy to staging and re-verify.
  5. Obtain written UAT sign-off.
OutputsUAT feedback log; fixed defects; signed UAT acceptance.
ToolsStaging site, shared feedback sheet or issue tracker, screen recordings.
RisksUnstructured feedback; new scope disguised as bugs; unavailable client reviewers.
VerificationEach acceptance criterion marked pass or fail with evidence.
DocumentationUAT sign-off form in the project folder.
Approval authorityClient sponsor.

Gate 22

Written UAT acceptance before production deployment.

Stage 23 — Production Deployment

PurposeRelease the approved build to the live environment safely, with a rollback ready.
Responsible employeeDevOps engineer (execute); Technical Lead (go/no-go); Project Manager (client communication).
InputsUAT sign-off; deployment checklist (Appendix A7); backup; rollback plan.
Procedure
  1. Agree a low-traffic window and notify the client.
  2. Take a fresh backup and confirm it restores.
  3. Promote the exact staging image through the pipeline with manual approval; run migrations.
  4. Run smoke tests; watch logs, errors and latency for at least 30 minutes.
  5. Record evidence - time, version, approver, results; roll back immediately if the criteria fail.
OutputsLive system; deployment record; release tag.
ToolsCI/CD, cloud console (read-only after deploy), monitoring dashboards.
RisksUnplanned downtime; failed migration; forgotten configuration; no rollback.
VerificationPost-deployment checklist complete; first backup of production taken.
DocumentationDeployment log and release notes.
Approval authorityTechnical Lead (go/no-go); client sponsor (change window).

Stage 24 — DNS and Domain Configuration

PurposePoint the client's domain at the live system correctly without breaking email.
Responsible employeeDevOps engineer; client domain owner (access).
InputsDomain ownership details; DNS plan; production endpoint.
Procedure
  1. Document the current DNS records (screenshot/export) before any change.
  2. Lower TTL to 300 seconds at least 24 hours before cut-over.
  3. Add or change A/AAAA/CNAME records; keep MX, SPF, DKIM, DMARC unchanged unless planned.
  4. Configure www and apex redirects; set canonical host.
  5. Verify from multiple resolvers; raise TTL after stability.
OutputsLive domain; DNS record table; email confirmed working.
ToolsRegistrar/Cloudflare, dig, nslookup, mail test tools.
RisksEmail outage; wrong record; domain registered in an employee's name.
Verificationdig from at least two public resolvers returns the intended records; test email sent and received.
DocumentationDNS record table and registrar details in docs/deployment.md.
Approval authorityTechnical Lead; client domain owner.

Stage 25 — SSL/TLS Verification

PurposeConfirm all traffic is encrypted with a valid, auto-renewing certificate and a sound configuration.
Responsible employeeDevOps engineer.
InputsLive domain; certificate source (Let's Encrypt, cloud-managed, Cloudflare, paid certificate if required).
Procedure
  1. Confirm HTTPS works for apex and www; HTTP redirects to HTTPS.
  2. Check certificate chain, expiry date and automatic renewal.
  3. Test with SSL Labs/Qualys server test and Mozilla Observatory; fix weak protocols.
  4. Add HSTS only after confirming no HTTP-only dependencies.
  5. Add certificate-expiry monitoring (alert at 21 and 7 days).
OutputsTLS report; renewal evidence; monitoring alert.
ToolsSSL Labs, openssl s_client, browser padlock details, uptime monitor.
RisksExpired certificate; mixed content; misconfigured redirect loop.
VerificationSSL Labs grade A or better; zero mixed-content warnings in DevTools.
DocumentationCertificate details and renewal method in docs/deployment.md.
Approval authorityTechnical Lead.

Stage 26 — Client Handover

PurposeTransfer ownership, knowledge and access so the client can run the system - or hand it to us on a managed plan.
Responsible employeeProject Manager; Technical Lead; DevOps engineer.
InputsLive system; documentation set; handover checklist (Appendix A8).
Procedure
  1. Deliver the documentation pack - architecture, database, API, deployment, security, user guide, runbooks.
  2. Transfer repository and cloud-account ownership as agreed; remove temporary access.
  3. Share credentials only through the approved secret manager or expiring secure link.
  4. Run a training session and record it; provide a quick-reference sheet.
  5. Obtain the signed handover/acceptance certificate and confirm the warranty start date.
OutputsDocumentation pack; ownership transfer record; training recording; signed handover certificate.
ToolsHandover checklist, password/secret manager, video call recording.
RisksCredentials in documents; missing runbooks; client cannot operate without us and does not know it.
VerificationClient performs three routine tasks (update content, create a user, restore a test backup) unaided.
DocumentationComplete docs/ folder and CHANGELOG.md at release version.
Approval authorityClient sponsor (acceptance); Project Manager (closure).

Gate 26

Signed handover certificate.

Stage 27 — Maintenance and Support

PurposeKeep the system secure, available and improving after launch under a clear service agreement.
Responsible employeeSupport lead / DevOps engineer; Project Manager for account management.
InputsSupport plan and SLA from the SOW; monitoring and ticket tools.
Procedure
  1. Monitor uptime, errors, certificates and backups; respond to alerts by agreed severity.
  2. Apply security patches and dependency updates monthly (critical issues in the agreed window) through staging first.
  3. Test a restore quarterly; review cost and performance monthly.
  4. Handle support tickets with first-response and resolution targets; classify bug vs change request.
  5. Send a monthly report; review renewal and improvement roadmap quarterly.
OutputsMonthly service report; patch log; restore-test log; renewal proposal.
